questions.title: Constant-Product vs. Concentrated Liquidity Curve Design
questions.prompt: Compare a constant-product AMM curve (x*y=k) with a concentrated-liquidity design like Uniswap v3's. What capital-efficiency and risk tradeoffs does concentrating liquidity into a price range actually introduce for liquidity providers and for protocol design?
questions.modelAnswer: A constant-product curve spreads an LP's capital across the entire price range from zero to infinity, which is simple and always has liquidity at any price but is capital-inefficient — most of that capital sits unused far from the current price. Concentrated liquidity lets an LP choose a price range to deposit into, so the same capital provides far deeper liquidity near the current price, improving quoted prices and reducing slippage for traders. The tradeoff is that an LP's position stops earning fees entirely once price exits their chosen range, and they're now effectively holding whichever asset the market moved away from — a sharper, range-bound version of impermanent loss that requires active range management. For protocol design, concentrated liquidity means the AMM has to track liquidity as a function of price in discretized ticks rather than one global reserve pair, which is materially more complex to implement correctly and to reason about for invariant testing, and it shifts risk from 'the protocol' to 'the LP's own range-management skill,' which changes who the protocol needs to protect against adverse outcomes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it as a capital-efficiency-versus-complexity tradeoff. With x*y=k, every LP is implicitly quoting at every price from zero to infinity, so most of their capital is dead weight sitting at prices the asset will probably never reach. Concentrated liquidity fixes that by letting LPs bet on a range, which means way deeper liquidity exactly where trading actually happens — that's why v3-style AMMs post tighter spreads with less total capital. But I always push back when a design treats that as a free upgrade: once price walks outside your range, you're earning zero fees and sitting in the worse-performing asset until someone actively rebalances you, which is a much sharper form of IL than a full-range position ever sees. On the engineering side, this is also where a lot of real bugs live — once you're tracking liquidity per tick instead of one reserve pair, the math for fee accounting, position NFTs, and crossing ticks during a swap gets genuinely hard to get right, and that's exactly where I'd want heavier invariant and fuzz test coverage before trusting it with real funds.
commonMistakes: Describes concentrated liquidity as strictly better without naming the range-exit risk
Doesn't connect concentrated liquidity to a sharper form of impermanent loss
Ignores the implementation complexity of tick-based accounting
Treats capital efficiency gains as free rather than a tradeoff against active management burden
keyPoints: Explains why full-range liquidity is capital-inefficient
Explains how concentrating liquidity improves depth/slippage near the current price
Identifies the range-exit risk and its relationship to impermanent loss
Notes the added implementation and testing complexity of tick-based liquidity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies range-exit risk as sharper IL

questions.title: Quantifying and Hedging Impermanent Loss
questions.prompt: Walk through how you'd actually quantify impermanent loss for a given pool and price move, and explain what real hedging or mitigation strategies are available to a sophisticated LP or to protocol designers trying to reduce it structurally.
questions.modelAnswer: Impermanent loss is the gap between the value of LP tokens and the value of simply holding the underlying assets, and for a constant-product pool it has a closed-form expression in terms of the price ratio change: loss grows with the square of how far price has diverged from the deposit price, so a 4x move in either direction produces a much larger loss than a 2x move, not twice as much. Quantifying it requires simulating or calculating the LP's position value at the new price versus a HODL baseline at the same price, not just looking at fees earned. Mitigation options include choosing pools with correlated assets (stablecoin-stablecoin or similar-beta pairs), where price divergence is structurally limited; using concentrated liquidity to earn more fee income per unit of capital to offset expected IL; and some protocols implementing IL protection mechanisms that top up LPs from a treasury or insurance fund, which shifts the risk rather than eliminating it. True hedging — shorting the volatile asset externally to offset the LP's effective short-gamma exposure — is possible but adds counterparty and funding-rate complexity most LPs don't actually manage well.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never let 'impermanent loss' stay abstract in an interview or in a design doc — I want the actual number. For a 50/50 constant-product pool, the formula compares your pooled value at the new price ratio to what you'd have if you'd just held both assets, and the key intuition people miss is that it scales roughly with the square of the price ratio change, so small moves cost you very little and big moves cost you a lot, nonlinearly. When I'm advising on mitigation, the first and best lever is picking which pool you're even in — correlated-asset pools like stable-stable pairs have way less divergence risk by construction, so that's often a better fix than any clever hedge. Past that, concentrated liquidity can help because you're earning denser fees to offset expected IL, but it's not a cure. I'm skeptical of protocols that promise 'IL protection' funded from a treasury, because that's not eliminating the loss, it's socializing it onto token holders or an insurance pool, and I'd want to know exactly how that fund is capitalized before calling it a real mitigation versus a marketing line. Actual external hedging with short positions works in theory but most LPs never maintain the funding-rate and rebalancing discipline required to make it net positive.
commonMistakes: Describes IL only qualitatively without the nonlinear/squared relationship to price divergence
Confuses fees earned with IL being 'cancelled out' without actually netting the two
Presents treasury-funded IL protection as eliminating risk rather than shifting it
Doesn't mention correlated-asset pool selection as the most practical mitigation
keyPoints: Gives a correct, concrete way to quantify IL versus a HODL baseline
Notes the nonlinear (roughly squared) relationship to price divergence
Names correlated-asset pools as a structural mitigation
Critically evaluates treasury-funded IL protection as risk-shifting, not risk-removal

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Critical evaluation of protocol-level IL protection schemes

questions.title: Designing a Kinked Utilization-Based Interest Rate Model
questions.prompt: Design an interest rate model for a lending protocol that uses a kinked, utilization-based curve. Explain why the kink exists, how you'd set the kink point and slopes, and what happens to the protocol if you get those parameters wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: A kinked model sets borrow (and derived supply) interest rates as a function of pool utilization — borrowed divided by supplied — with a gentle slope below a target utilization point and a much steeper slope above it. The kink exists because the protocol needs two different jobs done by the same mechanism: below target utilization, rates should rise gently to balance supply and demand without scaring off borrowers; above target utilization, the pool is at real risk of running out of liquidity for withdrawals, so rates need to spike sharply to aggressively pull utilization back down by discouraging new borrowing and incentivizing repayment or new deposits. Setting the kink point requires balancing capital efficiency (a higher target lets more of deposited capital actually get lent out and earn yield) against liquidity risk (a higher target leaves a thinner buffer before the pool can't service withdrawals). Getting the slopes wrong is dangerous in both directions: too flat above the kink and the pool can get stuck near 100% utilization with no mechanism pulling it back, risking a liquidity crunch where depositors can't withdraw; too steep below the kink and borrowing becomes unpredictably expensive on small utilization swings, driving away legitimate borrowers and starving the protocol of fee revenue.
questions.professionalAnswer: The kink is doing two jobs with one knob, and I always explain it that way. Under normal conditions you want borrow rates to nudge utilization toward a target gently — nobody should get a rate shock because utilization moved from 60 to 65 percent. But once you're past that target and heading toward 100 percent utilization, the pool is one large withdrawal away from depositors not being able to get their money out, and at that point rates need to get aggressive fast, which is the steep side of the kink pulling new borrowing down and existing borrowers toward repaying. Setting the actual kink point is a capital-efficiency-versus-safety call — push it up near 90 percent and you're lending out more of the deposited capital, which is great for yield, but you've shrunk the liquidity buffer before things get dangerous. I've seen protocols get this wrong in both directions: too flat above the kink and utilization camps at 99 percent during a market stress event with withdrawals queued up and no real lever to fix it; too steep below the kink and borrowers get whipsawed by rate swings on routine utilization noise and just leave for a competitor with calmer rates. In practice I'd backtest the curve against real historical utilization and withdrawal patterns before shipping it, not just pick numbers that look reasonable on a whiteboard.

Doesn't connect high utilization to actual withdrawal/liquidity risk for depositors
Treats kink-point selection as arbitrary rather than a capital-efficiency/safety tradeoff
Doesn't describe failure modes of a mis-set curve in either direction
keyPoints: Explains the gentle-slope vs steep-slope purposes of the kink
Connects high utilization directly to withdrawal/liquidity risk
Frames kink-point selection as a capital efficiency vs. safety tradeoff
Describes concrete failure modes of a badly tuned curve

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the purpose of the kink
Sound reasoning on setting the kink point and slopes
Identifies real failure modes of mis-tuned parameters

questions.title: Designing a Liquidation Engine That Survives Volatility
questions.prompt: Explain the core components of a liquidation engine for an overcollateralized lending protocol, and what specifically breaks when it's designed to only handle calm markets rather than sharp volatility spikes.
questions.modelAnswer: A liquidation engine needs a health-factor calculation (collateral value times liquidation threshold, divided by debt value) that can be evaluated cheaply on-chain, a trigger condition for when a position becomes liquidatable, an incentive (a liquidation bonus or discount) large enough to attract liquidators to actually do the work, and a price source feeding collateral valuation that is itself manipulation-resistant. What breaks under sharp volatility is usually a chain of failures: price oracles that update on a lag or are vulnerable to manipulation during exactly the fast-moving window when accurate pricing matters most; liquidator incentives that assume normal gas prices and normal competition, which collapse when gas spikes during network congestion and liquidators can't profitably execute; and insufficient liquidation bonus sizing that was calibrated against historical volatility rather than tail-risk scenarios, leaving positions under-liquidated and the protocol holding bad debt once collateral value falls below the debt it's supposed to cover. A robust design needs partial liquidations rather than all-or-nothing, a liquidation bonus that can flex or that's sized against worst-case historical drawdowns rather than average volatility, and ideally a backstop mechanism (a protocol-owned liquidation module or insurance fund) for positions that go underwater faster than external liquidators can respond.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pieces are straightforward on paper: you need a health factor, a threshold that triggers liquidation, a bonus that makes it worth someone's time to liquidate, and a price feed to value the collateral. The part that actually matters is what happens when all of that gets stress-tested in a crash instead of a calm market. First thing I check in any design is the oracle — if it updates on any kind of lag, or can be nudged by someone with enough capital during exactly the ten minutes a position needs liquidating, you've got a design that works great until the day it doesn't. Second is liquidator economics under congestion — a bonus sized for a 2% drawdown day doesn't cover gas costs when the network is jammed and everyone's trying to liquidate at once, so liquidators just sit it out and bad debt accumulates. I've seen protocols get burned specifically because they calibrated the liquidation bonus against average historical volatility instead of the worst day on record. My bar for a liquidation engine is: does it support partial liquidations instead of all-or-nothing, is the bonus sized against tail-risk history rather than an average, and is there some backstop — a protocol-run liquidation bot or insurance module — for the gap between 'theoretically liquidatable' and 'an external liquidator actually showed up in time.'

Doesn't connect oracle lag/manipulation risk to liquidation timing
Ignores liquidator gas-cost economics under network congestion
Calibrates liquidation bonus against average rather than tail-risk volatility

Identifies oracle lag/manipulation as a key failure point under volatility
Discusses liquidator economics breaking down under gas spikes/congestion
Proposes partial liquidations and tail-risk-calibrated bonuses as mitigations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes sound mitigations (partial liquidation, tail-risk sizing, backstop)

questions.title: Flash Loans: Mechanics and the Attack Surface They Create
questions.prompt: Explain how flash loans work mechanically, why they're not inherently malicious, and walk through the general shape of a flash-loan-enabled attack against a DeFi protocol — what makes these attacks possible and how protocols defend against them.
questions.modelAnswer: A flash loan lets a borrower take an uncollateralized loan of any size, as long as it's borrowed and fully repaid (plus a fee) within the same transaction — if repayment fails, the entire transaction, including the loan, reverts atomically, so the lender bears zero default risk. This is a genuinely useful primitive for arbitrage, collateral swaps, and self-liquidation, but it also hands an attacker temporary access to enormous capital with no upfront cost, which turns otherwise-minor logic flaws into large-scale exploits. The general attack shape is: borrow a huge sum via flash loan, use it to manipulate some state the target protocol trusts within that same transaction — most commonly a price that's read from a thinly-traded on-chain pool rather than a robust oracle, or a governance snapshot used for voting power — then exploit the target protocol's mispriced or misweighted state to drain value, and finally repay the flash loan, keeping the profit, all inside one atomic transaction. Defenses include never pricing collateral or triggering critical logic off a single, manipulable on-chain spot price; using time-weighted average prices or external oracle networks that aren't moveable within a single block; and, for governance, requiring voting power to be based on a snapshot taken before the proposal rather than current balance, so a flash-loaned token position can't swing a vote.
questions.professionalAnswer: Mechanically, a flash loan is just atomicity doing the work a credit check normally would — you can borrow basically unlimited capital with zero collateral because the EVM guarantees that if you don't pay it back by the end of the transaction, the whole thing including the loan never happened. That's legitimately useful for things like arbitrage or moving collateral between positions without needing bridge capital upfront. The reason it's also a weapon is that it turns 'this protocol trusts a manipulable price or snapshot' into a free, massive attack, because the attacker doesn't need their own capital to move that price - they just borrow it for one block. The classic shape I'd walk through in an interview is: flash-borrow a huge amount, dump or buy against a thin on-chain pool to swing its spot price, hit a target protocol that reads that exact pool as its oracle, exploit the now-wrong valuation to borrow more than they should or get an undercollateralized position approved, unwind, repay the flash loan, and walk away with the delta - all in one transaction nobody can intervene on mid-flight. The fix isn't banning flash loans, it's never trusting anything manipulable within a single block or transaction as ground truth - TWAP or external oracle feeds for pricing, and snapshot-based voting power taken before a proposal exists for governance, so there's no single atomic window an attacker can exploit.
commonMistakes: Frames flash loans themselves as inherently malicious rather than a neutral primitive
Doesn't explain the atomicity guarantee that makes zero-collateral lending safe for the lender
Describes the attack vaguely without naming the manipulated state (price oracle or governance snapshot)
Proposes banning flash loans rather than fixing the underlying trust-in-manipulable-state flaw
keyPoints: Correctly explains atomicity as the mechanism making flash loans safe for lenders
Acknowledges legitimate uses (arbitrage, collateral swaps, self-liquidation)
Walks through the borrow-manipulate-exploit-repay attack shape concretely
Names TWAP/external oracles and snapshot-based governance as the real defenses

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains flash loan mechanics and atomicity

questions.title: Token Supply Models and Their Long-Run Incentive Effects
questions.prompt: Compare fixed-supply, inflationary, and deflationary (burn-based) token supply models. What long-run incentive and valuation effects does each create for holders, and how does the choice interact with a protocol's need to pay for ongoing security or liquidity incentives?
questions.modelAnswer: A fixed-supply model gives holders certainty about dilution, which is attractive for a store-of-value narrative, but it means the protocol has no native mechanism to continuously fund security spending (like staking rewards) or ongoing liquidity incentives without either front-loading a huge initial allocation or relying on external revenue. An inflationary model — minting new tokens on a schedule to pay stakers, validators, or liquidity providers — solves the funding problem directly but dilutes existing holders continuously, and if the inflation rate isn't tied to real usage or revenue, it becomes a transfer from long-term holders to whoever is currently farming, eroding trust over time. A deflationary or burn-based model, where a portion of fees or supply is destroyed, creates a narrative of increasing scarcity and can align incentives if the burn is tied to genuine usage (fees burned scale with real activity), but if burn is disconnected from usage and instead just scheduled, it's cosmetic. In practice, mature protocols often blend these: inflationary rewards that taper over time to bootstrap security and liquidity, offset partially by fee-driven burns once usage is established, so early inflation funds growth while later burn mechanics reward the holders who stuck around once the protocol is self-sustaining.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this less as 'which model is best' and more as 'what is this token actually paying for.' Fixed supply is clean and easy to market as scarce, but it means you have no lever to keep paying validators or liquidity providers once any initial treasury runs out, unless the protocol has real external revenue. Inflationary models solve that funding problem honestly — you're minting to pay for security or liquidity, full stop — but I always want to know if the inflation rate is tied to anything real, like usage or revenue, because untethered inflation is just a quiet tax on whoever isn't actively farming the new issuance. Burn mechanics get marketed as deflationary and bullish, but I'm skeptical unless the burn scales with genuine protocol usage — fees burned because people are actually using the thing — versus a scheduled burn that's disconnected from activity and is really just a narrative device. The pattern I respect most in practice is a taper: start with meaningful inflation to bootstrap security and liquidity when the protocol has nothing else to offer, and design that inflation to decay over time as fee-driven burn or revenue sharing takes over, so the token's long-run value isn't permanently dependent on diluting new holders to pay old ones.

Doesn't connect inflation to the real need to fund security/liquidity incentives
Describes burn mechanics as automatically bullish without checking if it's usage-tied
Misses the common hybrid/tapering pattern used by mature protocols

Explains inflation's dilution risk when untethered from usage/revenue
Distinguishes usage-tied burn from scheduled/cosmetic burn

questions.title: Vesting Schedules and Cliffs as Governance-Attack Prevention
questions.prompt: Beyond preventing early team/investor dumps, explain how vesting schedule and cliff design also functions as a defense against governance attacks and short-term speculative control of a protocol. What specific design choices matter most?
questions.modelAnswer: Vesting is usually framed as anti-dump protection, but it also directly limits how much effective voting power can concentrate quickly in the hands of someone with no long-term stake in the protocol, because unvested tokens either shouldn't carry voting rights at all, or if they do, that's itself a design risk worth scrutinizing — a large unvested allocation with live governance rights is a latent concentration-of-power problem even before any tokens are liquid. The specific choices that matter most are: whether unvested tokens can vote at all (the safer default is no); the cliff length, which determines how long a new large holder (a team, investor, or treasury recipient) is locked in before they have any ability to exit, forcing genuine alignment during the protocol's most fragile early period; and the vesting curve shape after the cliff — linear vesting over a long tail is harder to game than a single large unlock, because a single unlock creates one specific date where a large voting bloc becomes liquid and could coordinate a sell-off or a governance power grab around that known event. Protocols that get this wrong often discover the problem only when a cliff date approaches and the community realizes a single wallet is about to receive both full liquidity and full voting power simultaneously, with no granular unlock in between.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dump-protection framing is the one everyone talks about, but the governance angle is the one I actually worry about more as an engineer. If unvested tokens carry voting rights, you've effectively given someone with zero long-term exposure to the protocol real control over its decisions right now, which is a mismatch I'd flag immediately in a design review — my default position is unvested tokens shouldn't vote, period, unless there's a specific and well-justified reason. Cliffs matter beyond 'can't sell yet' because they also mean 'can't exit the relationship yet,' which forces real alignment during the period the protocol is most fragile. The design detail people get wrong most often is the unlock shape after the cliff - a single cliff-end unlock creates one calendar date where a huge voting-capable, now-liquid bloc appears all at once, and that's exactly the kind of predictable event a sophisticated actor can plan a governance attack or a coordinated sell-off around. I always push for linear or stepped vesting after the cliff instead of one big unlock, specifically because it removes that single point-in-time concentration event and makes the token's voting power grow gradually and predictably instead of in one disruptive jump.

Assumes unvested tokens voting is normal/acceptable without flagging the risk
Doesn't connect cliff-end single unlocks to a predictable governance-attack window
No distinction between linear/stepped vesting and single-point unlocks
keyPoints: Connects vesting design to governance-power concentration, not just price dumps
Takes a clear position on unvested-token voting rights

questions.title: Flash-Loan Governance Attacks and Voting Power Design
questions.prompt: Explain how a flash-loan-based governance attack works against a naively designed on-chain voting system, and what specific delegation and snapshot mechanics prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer: A naive governance design that checks a voter's current token balance at the moment a vote is cast is vulnerable to a flash-loan attack: an attacker flash-borrows a large quantity of the governance token, uses that borrowed balance to cast a decisive vote (or to pass a malicious proposal outright) within the same transaction, and then repays the loan, all before the loan ever needs to be held for longer than one block — the attacker never had genuine long-term exposure to the token at all. The defense is to base voting power on a snapshot of balances taken at proposal creation time (or some block prior to it), not on live balance at voting time, so a flash-loaned balance acquired after the snapshot block simply doesn't count, no matter how large it is. Delegation adds another layer: many governance tokens use a checkpoint-based delegation system (recording historical voting power per address per block) specifically so that 'voting power as of block N' can be looked up cheaply and verifiably on-chain, rather than the contract needing to trust a live, manipulable balance. A secondary defense many protocols add is a minimum proposal-to-vote time delay, which further ensures no single-transaction attack can both create favorable conditions and vote on them.
questions.professionalAnswer: The naive version of this bug is almost funny once you see it: if 'how much voting power do you have' is just 'what's your current balance,' then anyone can borrow a mountain of tokens for one transaction, vote with them, and give the loan back before anyone's even finished reading the proposal. The fix that's now basically standard is snapshotting - voting power gets locked in as of a specific block, usually the block the proposal was created, so anything an attacker flash-borrows after that point is worthless for voting no matter how big the balance is. The mechanism that makes this cheap and trustworthy on-chain is checkpointed delegation - instead of reading a live balance, the token contract keeps a history of voting power per address per block, so 'what was this address's voting power at block N' is a verifiable lookup, not something that can be gamed by a transaction that happens after the fact. I'd also mention the belt-and-suspenders layer a lot of mature DAOs add: a mandatory delay between a proposal being created and voting actually opening, which closes off any attack that depends on creating a favorable condition and voting on it within the same breath.

Doesn't name snapshotting at proposal-creation time as the core fix
Omits checkpoint-based delegation as the mechanism that makes snapshotting practical
Misses the proposal-to-vote delay as a secondary defense

Explains snapshotting at proposal creation as the primary fix
Describes checkpoint-based delegation mechanics
Mentions proposal-to-vote delay as additional defense

questions.title: Timelocks and Multisig Treasuries as Layered Defense
questions.prompt: Explain why a DAO treasury or protocol upgrade mechanism should use both a multisig and a timelock, rather than either alone. What specific attack or failure does each layer stop that the other doesn't?
questions.modelAnswer: A multisig alone defends against a single compromised key being enough to move funds or push an upgrade, by requiring a threshold of independent signers, but it does nothing to protect against a majority of signers being compromised, colluding, or simply making a mistake together — if enough signers agree, the action executes immediately with no window for anyone outside that group to notice or react. A timelock alone defends against exactly that: even a fully authorized, correctly-signed action has to sit for a mandatory delay before it executes, giving the community, security researchers, or affected users a window to notice something is wrong (a malicious or buggy proposal) and react — by exiting the protocol, raising an alarm, or in extreme cases pushing a counter-governance action — before it takes effect. But a timelock alone doesn't improve the quality of who can propose or approve the action in the first place; without a multisig layer requiring several independent approvals, a single compromised proposer key could queue a malicious action that the timelock will, after its delay, happily execute, since the timelock enforces a delay, not correctness or legitimacy. Combined, the multisig raises the bar for getting a malicious action authorized at all, and the timelock ensures that even a successfully authorized malicious action still has a public, reactable delay before it's irreversible.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always explain this as two completely different failure modes being covered, not redundant protection. The multisig's job is making sure one bad actor or one leaked key can't do anything on its own — you need several independent people to agree, so compromising or colluding with just one signer isn't enough. But a multisig doesn't help you if a majority of those signers get socially engineered, compromised together, or just genuinely agree to something harmful - the action goes through instantly with no outside visibility. That's the gap the timelock closes: even once an action is fully, legitimately approved by the multisig, it has to wait out a mandatory delay before it actually executes, which gives the community or security researchers a real window to notice 'wait, this upgrade does something it shouldn't' and react before it's permanent. The part I'd stress in an interview is that neither one substitutes for the other - a timelock with no multisig means one compromised proposer key can still queue something malicious, it just takes longer to land; a multisig with no timelock means a fully authorized bad decision executes instantly with zero public reaction window. You want both: multisig raises the bar on getting something authorized, timelock guarantees even authorized actions are publicly inspectable before they're irreversible.

questions.title: Designing Reward Emission Schedules That Don't Collapse
questions.prompt: Explain the common failure pattern where a yield farming protocol's reward emissions attract mercenary capital that leaves as soon as emissions taper, and how you'd design an emission schedule and incentive structure to avoid that collapse.
questions.modelAnswer: The classic failure pattern is a high, flat, or front-loaded emission rate that attracts capital purely chasing the emission APY, with no intrinsic reason to stay once that APY drops — as soon as the schedule tapers or a better-emitting farm appears elsewhere, that capital exits en masse, often causing a liquidity or price cascade on the way out since it was never there for protocol-native reasons. Designing against this requires separating 'bootstrap' emissions from 'sustaining' incentives: an initial, clearly time-boxed and decaying emission schedule (often an exponential or stepped taper) used explicitly to attract initial liquidity and usage, paired with lock-up or vesting on the rewards themselves (rewards that vest over time rather than being immediately liquid and sellable) so recipients have a cost to exiting quickly. Longer-term sustainability comes from tying ongoing rewards to real revenue generation — fee sharing funded by actual protocol usage rather than token emissions — so that once the bootstrap period ends, the incentive to stay isn't 'the subsidy is still generous' but 'the protocol genuinely generates value I'm sharing in.' Transparent, published decay schedules known in advance also matter, because capital that knows exactly when and how much emissions will drop can plan accordingly rather than being surprised into a panic exit.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the mercenary-capital problem and I've watched it play out the same way more than once: emissions start high to bootstrap liquidity, they work great for a few weeks, then the schedule tapers or a new farm offers better APY elsewhere, and the capital that was only ever there for the subsidy leaves all at once, often tanking the token price and draining liquidity right when the protocol needs it most. The fix I'd design in from day one is treating emissions as a bootstrap tool with an explicit end state, not an ongoing subsidy - a published, decaying schedule that everyone can see coming, so there's no surprise cliff that triggers a panic exit. I'd pair that with vesting on the rewards themselves, not just the token's own vesting - if your farming rewards unlock over weeks instead of landing fully liquid immediately, mercenary capital has a real cost to hit-and-run farming, which filters for participants willing to stick around. The actual long-term fix, though, is making sure there's something real to stay for once the bootstrap period ends - fee-sharing funded by genuine usage, not more emissions - so the pitch to a liquidity provider six months in isn't 'the subsidy is still good' but 'this protocol actually generates revenue and I'm getting a piece of it.'

Doesn't propose vesting/lockups on rewards as a specific mitigation
Doesn't distinguish bootstrap emissions from sustainable, revenue-based incentives
Misses the value of a transparent, pre-published decay schedule

questions.title: Fuzz Testing vs. Invariant Testing: What Each Actually Proves
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between fuzz testing and invariant testing for smart contracts. Why is it a mistake to treat them as interchangeable, and what does a mature test suite need from each?
questions.modelAnswer: Fuzz testing generates random or semi-random inputs to a specific function and checks that function's behavior against assertions for that single call — it's excellent at finding edge cases in input handling (overflow conditions, boundary values, unexpected reverts) within one function's scope. Invariant testing is a different question entirely: it defines properties that must hold true of the system's overall state across arbitrary sequences of calls, in any order, with any actors, and then a fuzzer-driven engine executes long random call sequences checking that the invariant never breaks at any point. The mistake is assuming thorough fuzz testing of individual functions implies the system as a whole is safe, when most real-world exploits come from the interaction between functions and state over a sequence of calls — a reentrancy bug, an accounting mismatch that only appears after a specific multi-step sequence, or a state that becomes inconsistent only after calls happen in an order no single-function fuzz test would ever construct. A mature suite needs fuzz tests to harden individual function boundaries and invariant tests to continuously verify system-wide properties (like 'total supply always equals the sum of balances' or 'the protocol is always solvent') hold no matter what sequence of actions, including adversarial ones, gets thrown at it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw a sharp line here because I've seen teams genuinely confuse the two and think heavy fuzzing means they're covered. Fuzz testing is about one function at a time — throw a huge range of random inputs at `withdraw` or `swap` and check it never does something it shouldn't for any single call. That's valuable and catches real bugs, but it's fundamentally a single-call lens. Invariant testing asks a completely different question: no matter what sequence of calls happens, in what order, by what actors, does some property of the whole system stay true — total supply equals sum of balances, the protocol never goes insolvent, nobody can withdraw more than they deposited. The exploits I actually worry about almost never come from one function misbehaving on a weird input; they come from a sequence of otherwise-valid calls that leaves the system in a state nobody designed for. So when I'm reviewing a test suite, fuzz coverage on individual functions is table stakes, but what actually tells me the team understands risk is whether they've written real invariants and let an invariant-testing engine hammer the whole contract with long random call sequences trying to break those properties, because that's the closest thing to simulating an actual adversary.
commonMistakes: Treats fuzz testing and invariant testing as interchangeable or redundant
Describes fuzz testing without noting its single-function scope
Doesn't explain that invariants hold across arbitrary call sequences
Misses that most real exploits come from multi-call state interactions, not single-call edge cases

Explains invariants as properties holding across arbitrary call sequences
Connects real-world exploits to multi-call state issues, not single-call bugs
States that a mature suite needs both, for different reasons

questions.title: What Test Coverage Doesn't Tell You — and Where Formal Verification Fits
questions.prompt: A smart contract has 100% line and branch coverage from its test suite. Explain why that number alone tells you very little about its actual security, and describe where formal verification concepts fit into closing that gap.
questions.modelAnswer: Coverage measures whether a line or branch was executed at least once by some test, not whether the test asserted anything meaningful about the result, and it says nothing about combinations of state or call sequences the suite never constructed — a function can be 'covered' by a test that calls it with benign inputs while a completely different, adversarial input or call sequence triggers a bug the suite never exercised. 100% coverage is a floor, not a ceiling: it rules out dead code and totally untested paths, but it doesn't rule out wrong assertions, missing edge cases within a covered line, or emergent bugs from interactions between functions. Formal verification addresses a fundamentally different question: instead of testing specific inputs, it mathematically proves (or disproves) that a property holds for all possible inputs and states within the model, using tools like symbolic execution or theorem proving to exhaustively reason about the contract's logic rather than sampling it. In practice, most teams use formal verification selectively on the highest-risk, highest-value logic — the core invariant-critical paths like accounting, access control, or liquidation math — rather than the whole codebase, because formal methods are expensive in tooling and specification effort, and pairing exhaustive proof on critical paths with fuzz/invariant testing on the broader system gives much stronger assurance than either alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: 100% coverage is a number I take with real skepticism, because it only tells you every line got executed at least once, not that any test actually checked the right thing happened. I can write a test that calls a function and asserts nothing meaningful, and that line is now 'covered.' Coverage also says nothing about the combinations the suite never thought to try — the adversarial input, the weird call order, the edge case between two covered branches that was never actually hit together. So I treat coverage as a floor that rules out obviously dead or entirely untested code, not evidence of security. Formal verification is a genuinely different tool: instead of sampling inputs, you're mathematically proving a property holds for every possible input and state the model allows, which is a much stronger guarantee than any amount of testing can give you, because testing samples and formal verification proves. The realistic way I'd apply it isn't 'formally verify the whole contract' — that's expensive and the specification effort alone can rival writing the contract twice — it's picking the handful of properties that would be catastrophic if wrong, like solvency invariants or access control, and formally verifying those specifically, while leaning on fuzz and invariant testing for everything else. That combination is what actually gives me confidence, not a coverage percentage on its own.
commonMistakes: Treats 100% coverage as strong evidence of security
Doesn't explain that coverage measures execution, not correctness of assertions
Describes formal verification vaguely without the 'proof for all inputs vs. sampling' distinction
Suggests formally verifying an entire codebase rather than targeting high-risk properties
keyPoints: Explains what coverage actually measures and its limits
Distinguishes testing (sampling) from formal verification (proof)
Describes formal verification as targeted at high-risk, invariant-critical logic
Recommends combining targeted formal verification with broader fuzz/invariant testing

Correctly explains formal verification's proof-based approach

questions.title: Proxy Patterns and the Real Cost of Upgradeability
questions.prompt: Explain how a proxy-based upgradeable contract pattern works, and what specific new risks it introduces compared to an immutable contract — risks that don't exist at all for a contract that can never be upgraded.
questions.modelAnswer: A proxy pattern splits a contract's permanent address (which users and other contracts interact with) from its logic, which lives in a separate implementation contract that the proxy delegates calls to via delegatecall, executing the implementation's code in the proxy's own storage context; upgrading means pointing the proxy at a new implementation address without the user-facing address ever changing. This introduces risks that simply don't exist for immutable contracts: storage layout collisions, where a new implementation's variable layout doesn't match the old one's, corrupting state in subtle ways that may not even revert, just silently misread or miswrite data; function selector clashes between the proxy's own admin functions and the implementation's functions, which can let an attacker call an unintended function if signatures collide; and the upgrade mechanism itself becoming the single highest-value attack target in the whole system, since whoever controls the upgrade (or can trick/compromise whoever controls it) effectively controls the entire contract's logic going forward, retroactively over all existing funds and state. Mitigations include using well-audited standard proxy patterns (UUPS or transparent proxies) rather than custom ones, storage-layout tooling that checks compatibility before every upgrade, and gating the upgrade capability itself behind a multisig and timelock rather than a single key, treating 'who can upgrade' as the most security-critical question in the entire system.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanism is that the proxy is the permanent address everyone talks to, and it uses delegatecall to run the logic contract's code but in its own storage — so upgrading is just repointing which logic address the proxy delegates to, and the user-facing contract address never changes. That's genuinely useful, but I always tell teams considering it that you're not avoiding risk, you're trading one category of risk for a different, arguably scarier one. Storage layout mismatches are the classic silent killer — if the new implementation's variables don't line up slot-for-slot with the old one, you don't get a clean revert, you get corrupted state that might not surface until much later. Selector clashes are the other subtle one, where the proxy's own admin-facing functions can collide with implementation functions in a way that's exploitable. But honestly the thing I'd spend the most interview time on is that upgradeability concentrates risk into a single question: who can authorize an upgrade, and what happens if that key or process is compromised. An immutable contract simply doesn't have this attack surface at all - there's no upgrade path to hijack. So if I'm recommending a proxy pattern, I'm also recommending it comes with a well-audited standard implementation, automated storage-layout compatibility checks before every upgrade, and the upgrade capability itself locked behind a multisig and timelock, because that single control point is now the most valuable target in the entire system.
commonMistakes: Describes the proxy mechanism without naming storage layout collision risk
Doesn't mention function selector clashes as a risk category
Treats upgradeability as a free feature rather than a concentrated new attack surface
Doesn't propose governance (multisig/timelock) around the upgrade capability itself
keyPoints: Correctly explains the proxy/delegatecall mechanism
Identifies storage layout collision as a key new risk
Identifies function selector clashes as a risk category
Frames the upgrade-authorization mechanism itself as the highest-value attack target

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies storage layout and selector clash risks
Frames upgrade authorization as the key new attack surface

questions.title: The Oracle Problem and Manipulation-Resistant Design
questions.prompt: Explain the oracle problem in blockchain systems, and describe the specific design choices that make an oracle feed resistant to manipulation versus one that's an easy attack target.
questions.modelAnswer: The oracle problem is that a blockchain can only natively trust data produced by its own deterministic execution, but most useful applications (price-based lending, insurance, prediction markets) need real-world data that originates off-chain, and getting that data on-chain necessarily means trusting some entity or mechanism to report it honestly, reintroducing exactly the kind of trusted-intermediary risk blockchains were meant to avoid. An easy-to-attack oracle design reads a single source — commonly the spot price of a single, possibly thin, on-chain liquidity pool — which an attacker with enough capital (often via a flash loan) can manipulate within a single block or transaction, feeding the consuming protocol a wrong price for exactly as long as needed to exploit it. Manipulation-resistant design uses multiple independent data sources aggregated together so manipulating the feed requires simultaneously compromising several independent sources, not just one; time-weighted averaging so a price has to be sustained across multiple blocks rather than just one, defeating single-transaction manipulation; and decentralized oracle networks (like Chainlink) where independent node operators each report and the final value is derived from consensus among them with economic penalties for reporting incorrect data, making manipulation economically irrational rather than just technically possible. The core principle is that anything a single transaction or a single actor can move shouldn't be trusted as ground truth for any decision with real financial consequences.
questions.professionalAnswer: The oracle problem, stated plainly, is that the chain only knows what happened inside its own execution, and almost everything useful — a price, a weather event, an election result — happens outside it, so the moment you need that data on-chain, you've reintroduced trust in whoever's reporting it, which is the exact thing a lot of this technology was trying to get away from. The failure mode I see most in reviews is a protocol reading a single on-chain price, often from one thin liquidity pool, as its source of truth - that's an invitation for someone with a flash loan to move that price for one transaction and walk away with the difference. What actually makes an oracle resistant is layering several independent defenses: multiple independent sources aggregated together so no single feed's manipulation moves the final number much; time-weighting so a price has to hold across several blocks, not just one transaction, to matter; and for anything serious, a decentralized oracle network where multiple independent operators report and there's real economic stake backing honest reporting, so lying isn't just hard, it's expensive. The rule of thumb I give junior engineers is: if a single actor, in a single transaction, can move the number your contract is about to trust, that number isn't trustworthy, full stop, no matter how official the data source looks.
commonMistakes: Doesn't explain why the oracle problem exists (chain can only trust its own execution)
Describes a single-source price feed without identifying the manipulation risk
Doesn't mention time-weighted averaging as a defense against single-block manipulation
Omits decentralized oracle networks and their economic-penalty mechanism
keyPoints: Correctly explains why the oracle problem exists
Identifies single-source, single-block price reads as the key vulnerability
Describes multi-source aggregation and time-weighting as defenses
Explains decentralized oracle networks and economic penalties for bad reporting

questions.title: Chain Reorgs and Why Indexers Can't Just Trust the Latest Block
questions.prompt: Explain what a chain reorganization is, why it specifically breaks naive event-indexing code, and what design pattern an indexer needs to handle reorgs correctly.
questions.modelAnswer: A chain reorganization happens when a node's view of the canonical chain changes — a block (or several) that was previously considered part of the chain gets replaced by a different block at the same height, because the network reached consensus on a different fork, which is more common on probabilistic-finality chains and near the tip of the chain where confirmations are shallow. Naive indexing code that reads events from 'the latest block' and treats them as final breaks because it may process events from a block that later gets reorged out, meaning the indexer's database now contains events for transactions that, from the chain's current canonical perspective, never actually happened — producing phantom deposits, incorrect balances, or duplicate/missing records depending on how the reorg is (mis)handled. The correct pattern is to only treat data as final once it's behind a confirmation depth appropriate to the chain (waiting N blocks before treating an event as settled), and to design the indexer to detect reorgs explicitly — by tracking block hashes, not just numbers, and noticing when a previously-indexed block hash no longer matches the canonical chain at that height — and to roll back (invalidate) any indexed data from reorged-out blocks before reprocessing the new canonical chain's events for that range, rather than silently layering new data on top of stale data.
questions.professionalAnswer: A reorg is just the chain changing its mind about which block was canonical at some height — a different fork won out, and a block you'd already processed isn't part of the chain anymore. The reason naive indexers break on this is they treat 'I saw this event in a block' as permanent the moment they see it, so if that block gets reorged out, the indexer is now carrying phantom data for something that, as far as the chain is concerned right now, never happened. I've debugged exactly this — a deposit event indexed from a block that got reorged out, and now a user's balance reflects a deposit that doesn't exist on-chain anymore. The pattern that actually handles this correctly has two parts: first, don't treat anything as final until it's behind a sensible confirmation depth for that chain, because shallow, recent blocks are exactly where reorgs happen; second, track block hashes, not just block numbers, so the indexer can detect 'the block I have at height N doesn't match what's canonical anymore' and explicitly roll back everything indexed from that point before reprocessing the new canonical chain. Skipping that rollback step and just layering new events on top of stale ones is how you end up with duplicate or ghost records that take way longer to debug than building the rollback logic would have taken in the first place.
commonMistakes: Doesn't explain why reorgs happen or that they're more common near the chain tip
Describes the symptom (bad data) without explaining the root cause (treating unconfirmed blocks as final)
Doesn't mention tracking block hashes (not just numbers) to detect reorgs
Omits the need to explicitly roll back reorged-out data before reprocessing
keyPoints: Correctly explains what a chain reorg is and why it happens near the tip
Explains why treating unconfirmed data as final breaks naive indexers
Describes confirmation-depth waiting as a mitigation
Describes block-hash tracking and explicit rollback as the correct indexer pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes the correct confirmation-depth and rollback pattern

questions.title: The Graph / Subgraph Architecture for Indexing On-Chain Data
questions.prompt: Explain why you generally can't query rich, relational history directly from a blockchain node, and describe how The Graph's subgraph architecture (schema, mapping handlers, deployment) solves that problem.
questions.modelAnswer: A blockchain node is optimized for validating and executing transactions against current state, not for answering relational historical queries like 'give me all NFT sales by this collection in the last 30 days, sorted by price' — that kind of query would require scanning the entire event history and joining across multiple contracts and event types, which a node's RPC interface isn't built to do efficiently, if at all. The Graph's subgraph architecture solves this by defining a GraphQL schema describing the entities an application actually needs to query (a Sale entity, a Listing entity, with fields and relationships), then writing mapping handlers — functions triggered by specific on-chain events — that transform raw event data into writes against those schema-defined entities, maintained in an indexed, queryable datastore as new blocks arrive. Once deployed, the subgraph continuously processes new blocks, keeping its indexed entities current, and the application queries the subgraph's GraphQL endpoint instead of the chain directly, getting fast, relational, filterable results that would be impractical or impossible to get from raw RPC calls. This moves the 'hard query' problem off the hot path of the chain entirely and into a purpose-built indexing layer designed exactly for that job.
questions.professionalAnswer: The honest answer to 'why can't I just query the chain for this' is that a node is built to answer 'what is the current state' and 'is this transaction valid,' not 'show me every sale across three contracts in the last month sorted by price' — that's a relational, historical, cross-event query, and RPC nodes just aren't built to answer that efficiently, if they can answer it at all without you manually scanning and reconstructing history yourself. The subgraph model fixes this by letting you define upfront, in a GraphQL schema, exactly the shape of data your app actually needs — entities like Sale or Listing with the fields and relationships you care about — and then writing mapping handlers that listen for specific on-chain events and translate them into writes against those entities as blocks come in. Once that's deployed, you're not hitting the chain at query time at all, you're querying a purpose-built, already-indexed GraphQL endpoint that's been incrementally built up block by block. I think of it as moving all the expensive, relational work off the chain's hot path entirely and into infrastructure designed specifically for answering exactly the questions your app needs answered, which is the difference between a query that's fast and one that's effectively impossible.
commonMistakes: Doesn't explain specifically why node RPC interfaces can't answer relational/historical queries
Describes subgraphs vaguely without mentioning the schema-mapping-handler structure
Doesn't explain that mapping handlers are triggered by specific on-chain events
Fails to contrast querying the subgraph vs. querying the chain directly
keyPoints: Explains why raw chain/RPC queries can't efficiently answer relational history questions
Describes the GraphQL schema as defining the app's needed entities
Explains mapping handlers as event-triggered transforms into schema entities
Contrasts querying a purpose-built indexed endpoint vs. the chain directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why raw chain queries fall short
Clarity of the overall architecture explanation

questions.title: NFT Royalties and Marketplace Mechanics at Scale
questions.prompt: Explain how on-chain NFT royalty enforcement is supposed to work, why it's become unreliable across marketplaces in practice, and what design options exist for a marketplace or collection that genuinely wants royalties to be respected.
questions.modelAnswer: Royalty standards like EIP-2981 let a collection declare a royalty recipient and percentage that marketplaces are supposed to read and pay out on every secondary sale, but the standard is advisory, not enforced by the token contract itself — nothing in ERC-721 or ERC-1155 prevents a transfer from happening without a royalty payment, so royalty enforcement has always depended on marketplace goodwill rather than protocol-level guarantees. This became unreliable in practice once competing marketplaces realized they could attract sellers by not enforcing royalties (effectively letting sellers keep 100% of the sale price), creating a race to the bottom where marketplaces that honored royalties lost volume to ones that didn't, and peer-to-peer or aggregator-routed trades can bypass royalty-respecting marketplaces entirely. Design options for creators who want enforcement include operator filtering (restricting which marketplace contracts are allowed to call transfer functions on the collection, blocking non-compliant marketplaces at the contract level, though this is contentious since it limits where holders can freely trade), building royalties into the transfer function itself so a sale literally cannot complete without the royalty payment firing atomically, and accepting that any approach relying on marketplace compliance alone will eventually be circumvented by some venue, making contract-level enforcement the only approach with real teeth, at the cost of some flexibility for legitimate holders.
questions.professionalAnswer: The standard says royalties should work a specific way — EIP-2981 lets a collection declare who gets paid and how much on secondary sales — but the part people gloss over is that it's purely advisory. There's nothing in the ERC-721 transfer function that says 'you can't move this NFT unless the royalty got paid,' so enforcement has always been a matter of marketplaces choosing to honor it. That worked fine until marketplaces figured out that not enforcing royalties was a competitive advantage — sellers naturally gravitate to the venue where they keep more of the sale price — and once one major marketplace made royalties optional, it put pressure on everyone else to follow or lose volume. If a creator genuinely wants enforcement with teeth, relying on marketplace goodwill isn't a strategy anymore. The real options are contract-level: operator filtering, where the collection contract itself blocks transfer calls from marketplace contracts that don't enforce royalties, which works but is controversial because it restricts where legitimate holders can sell; or baking the royalty payment directly into the transfer path so the sale physically can't complete atomically without it firing. My honest take in an interview is that any enforcement strategy depending on marketplaces choosing to cooperate is fragile by design, and the only approach that survives a marketplace deciding not to cooperate is enforcement written into the contract itself.
commonMistakes: Assumes royalty standards are enforced at the protocol/token-contract level
Doesn't explain the market-dynamics reason enforcement eroded (competitive race to the bottom)
Doesn't mention operator filtering or contract-embedded royalty enforcement as real options
Fails to note the tradeoff operator filtering creates for legitimate holder flexibility
keyPoints: Correctly explains EIP-2981 as advisory, not enforced by the token standard
Explains the competitive-dynamics reason royalty enforcement eroded across marketplaces
Describes operator filtering and contract-embedded enforcement as real options
Acknowledges the tradeoff these enforcement options create

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains royalty standard mechanics and its advisory nature
Explains why enforcement eroded in practice

questions.title: Composability Risk: When Money Legos Become a Liability
questions.prompt: DeFi's 'money legos' composability is usually framed as a strength. Explain the specific risks that composability introduces when protocols build on top of each other, and how a protocol team should evaluate dependency risk before integrating with another protocol.
questions.modelAnswer: Composability lets protocols integrate with each other permissionlessly — a lending protocol accepting another protocol's LP tokens as collateral, a yield aggregator routing capital through several underlying protocols — which is powerful because it lets new functionality get built without needing to rebuild primitives from scratch, but it also means a protocol's security is no longer just a function of its own code; it inherits the risk of everything it depends on. The core danger is that a vulnerability or an economic failure in an underlying protocol can cascade upward: if a lending protocol accepts another protocol's token as collateral and that token's price mechanism gets exploited or its underlying protocol gets drained, the lending protocol's collateral valuations are suddenly wrong too, potentially triggering bad debt or a liquidity crisis it never directly caused. Evaluating dependency risk before integrating requires treating it like a real due-diligence process: reviewing the dependency's audit history and time-in-production (newer, unaudited protocols are categorically riskier dependencies), understanding what happens to your protocol's state and users if the dependency is paused, exploited, or behaves unexpectedly, and designing explicit circuit breakers or exposure caps so that a failure in one dependency is contained rather than able to drain the entire protocol. Treating 'it's composable, so we can just integrate' as sufficient diligence is how a well-audited protocol ends up losing user funds because of someone else's bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: I like composability as much as anyone building in this space, but I treat every integration with another protocol as taking on that protocol's risk profile as my own, not just borrowing its functionality for free. The failure pattern I watch for is cascading risk — if my lending protocol accepts another protocol's LP token or staking receipt as collateral, and that underlying protocol gets exploited or its price mechanism breaks, my protocol now has bad or mispriced collateral through no fault of my own code, and my users still bear the consequences. So before I'd sign off on integrating with another protocol, I want real due diligence: how long has it been live, what's its audit history actually look like, has it survived a real market stress event, not just a calm bull run. More importantly, I want to know exactly what happens to my protocol's users if that dependency gets paused or drained tomorrow — is the blast radius contained, or does it propagate straight through to insolvency on my side. That's where exposure caps and circuit breakers come in — I'd rather cap how much of my protocol's collateral can be any single external dependency, and have an automated or fast-manual way to pause that specific integration, than discover during an actual incident that 'composable' quietly meant 'our risk is now whoever we integrated with's risk, uncapped.'
commonMistakes: Describes composability only as a benefit without naming the inherited-risk problem
Doesn't give a concrete cascading-failure example
Proposes no concrete due-diligence process before integrating with a dependency
Doesn't mention exposure caps or circuit breakers as containment mechanisms
keyPoints: Explains composability's benefit alongside its inherited-risk cost
Gives a concrete cascading-failure scenario
Describes a real due-diligence process for evaluating a dependency
Proposes exposure caps/circuit breakers to contain dependency failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the inherited-risk nature of composability

questions.title: Implementing Slippage Protection in an AMM Swap Function
questions.prompt: Write (or describe precisely, in pseudocode/Solidity-style) a `swap` function for a constant-product AMM that protects callers against slippage and sandwich attacks. What parameters does the caller need to supply, and what does the function check before executing?
questions.modelAnswer: The caller must supply amountIn, a minAmountOut floor computed off-chain (typically the quoted output minus an acceptable slippage tolerance), the token being sold, a recipient address, and a deadline timestamp. Before executing, the function must check the deadline hasn't passed (protecting against a transaction sitting unmined in the mempool for a long time and executing against a stale price expectation), compute the actual output using the current reserves and the constant-product formula with the fee applied, and then hard-require that computed amountOut is at least minAmountOut, reverting the entire transaction atomically if not. This minAmountOut check is the actual slippage/sandwich protection: a sandwich attacker who front-runs the swap to move the price against the victim and back-runs it after will cause the victim's actual amountOut to fall below their specified floor, and the transaction simply reverts rather than executing at a bad price, so the attacker's front-run gains nothing from this victim's transaction (though the victim still pays gas for a reverted transaction, which is why tight minAmountOut combined with private/protected transaction submission is the more complete defense). The deadline check separately protects against a different problem: a transaction that waits unusually long before being mined, executing against reserves that have moved far from what the caller intended when they signed it.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I write this function, the two checks I never skip are the deadline and the minAmountOut floor, because together they're the entire slippage/sandwich defense — the AMM math itself doesn't protect you from anything. The deadline check exists because a signed transaction can sit in the mempool longer than expected and then execute against reserves that have drifted since the user quoted their trade, so I always require block.timestamp to be within the caller-specified deadline before touching reserves. The minAmountOut check is the one that actually stops a sandwich attack from draining the user — I compute the real output off current reserves after the fee, and if it's below what the caller said they'd accept, I revert the whole transaction, full stop, before any transfer happens. What I'd explain in a live-coding round is that this doesn't prevent a sandwich attempt from happening, it prevents it from succeeding against this specific transaction — the attacker's front-run and back-run still cost them gas and capital, and if the victim's minAmountOut is set tight to their quoted price, the squeeze either fails outright with a revert or isn't profitable enough for the attacker to bother. I'd also flag that minAmountOut has to be computed by the client against a fresh quote, not hardcoded, or you've just moved the vulnerability from the contract to wherever that number gets picked.
questions.example: A user expects 100 USDC for 1 ETH. They set minAmountOut to 99 USDC (1% slippage tolerance). An attacker sandwiches the trade, pushing the price so the user would only receive 95 USDC. The require(amountOut >= minAmountOut) check fails, the whole transaction reverts, and the user's funds never move — they only lose the gas for the failed transaction, not the 5 USDC they would have lost had the swap gone through.
commonMistakes: Omits the deadline check, leaving transactions vulnerable to execution long after being signed
Computes amountOut after transferring funds instead of before, breaking the revert-before-transfer guarantee
Hardcodes or omits minAmountOut entirely, providing no real slippage protection
Doesn't apply the fee before computing amountOut, producing an incorrect quote
keyPoints: Includes both deadline and minAmountOut as required parameters
Checks deadline before touching reserves
Computes amountOut correctly with fee applied, then requires it meets the floor before any transfer
Explains that this makes a sandwich unprofitable/failing for this transaction, not impossible to attempt

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct swap function logic and ordering of checks
Includes deadline protection and explains its purpose

questions.title: Implementing Health-Factor-Gated Liquidation in a Lending Pool
questions.prompt: Describe/write the core logic for a `liquidate` function in a simple overcollateralized lending pool: how it computes a borrower's health factor, what condition allows liquidation, and how the liquidator's incentive (bonus/discount) gets applied.
questions.modelAnswer: The health factor is computed as collateral value (priced via the oracle) multiplied by the liquidation threshold, divided by outstanding debt value; a health factor at or above 1.0 means the position is adequately collateralized, and below 1.0 means it's eligible for liquidation. The liquidate function must first assert the health factor is actually below the threshold — allowing liquidation of a healthy position would let a liquidator steal collateral from a solvent borrower, which is a critical invariant to enforce. A well-designed function also caps how much debt can be repaid in a single liquidation call (a partial liquidation limit, commonly 50%) rather than allowing full liquidation in one shot, which reduces the price impact and capital requirement for any single liquidator and makes the system liquidatable by more participants. The liquidator's incentive is applied by seizing collateral worth more than the debt repaid — the repaid amount plus a liquidation bonus percentage, converted to collateral units via the oracle price — so liquidators are compensated for the capital, gas, and risk involved in doing the liquidation, with the bonus coming out of the borrower's remaining collateral, not minted or subsidized by the protocol.
questions.professionalAnswer: The health factor calculation is the piece I'm most careful with, because getting the units wrong here is where real bugs live — collateral value and debt value both need to be in the same denomination (I always use USD-scaled 1e18 fixed point) before dividing, and I apply the liquidation threshold to collateral, not to debt, since the threshold represents how much of the collateral's value the protocol is willing to count toward solvency. The liquidate function's very first line has to be the health check — below 1.0 proceeds, at or above reverts — because skipping that is the single most catastrophic bug you can ship in a lending protocol; it lets anyone liquidate anyone, healthy or not. I always cap a single liquidation call to a fraction of the total debt, usually 50%, both because it limits how much capital or price impact any one liquidator needs and because full liquidations in one shot tend to produce worse execution for the borrower than they need to. The incentive mechanic is just making sure the liquidator walks away with collateral worth more than what they repaid — repay amount plus a bonus percentage, converted through the oracle price into collateral units — and I'm explicit in review that this bonus comes from the borrower's own collateral, it's not something the protocol treasury is funding, because that distinction matters for how you reason about protocol solvency afterward.
commonMistakes: Allows liquidation of a healthy (health factor >= 1.0) position
Mixes collateral and debt value units incorrectly (e.g. applying threshold to debt instead of collateral)
Allows unlimited single-transaction full liquidation with no partial-liquidation cap
Funds the liquidation bonus from protocol treasury rather than the borrower's own seized collateral
keyPoints: Correctly computes health factor using threshold-adjusted collateral over debt
Hard-requires health factor below 1.0 before allowing liquidation
Implements a partial liquidation cap
Correctly applies the liquidator bonus out of seized collateral, not protocol funds

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly gates liquidation on health factor

questions.title: Implementing a Timelock-Gated Governance Execution Function
questions.prompt: Write the core `queue` and `execute` logic for a simple governance contract that requires a proposal to pass a vote, then sit in a timelock before execution. What state needs to be tracked, and what checks must `execute` perform?
questions.modelAnswer: The contract needs to track, per proposal, a unique identifier, the target address and call data to execute, the eta (earliest execution timestamp, set to the queue time plus the mandatory delay), and an executed flag to prevent replay. Queue should only be callable after a proposal has genuinely passed its vote — gating that upstream — and should set eta to the current time plus the fixed delay, never allowing an eta in the past. Execute must check: the proposal actually exists (not a forged or unknown id); the current timestamp is at or past eta (the delay has actually elapsed, not just queued); critically, that the current timestamp hasn't exceeded eta plus a grace period, because without an upper bound a queued-but-forgotten malicious or stale proposal could sit indefinitely and be executed much later under completely different circumstances than when it was approved; and that it hasn't already been executed, preventing replay of the same action twice. The executed flag must be set before making the external call (checks-effects-interactions ordering), so a reentrant call during execution can't re-trigger execute on the same proposal.
questions.professionalAnswer: The state I track is deliberately minimal but each field is load-bearing: the eta is the earliest time this can execute, calculated once at queue time as now-plus-delay, never recalculated later, and an executed boolean that I set before making the external call, not after, specifically so a reentrant call can't slip through and execute the same proposal twice. The check I see teams forget most often in `execute` is the grace period — the upper bound on how long after eta a proposal can still be executed. Without that, you can have a proposal that passed a vote and got queued eight months ago, nobody remembered to execute or cancel it, and now it fires in a completely different market or governance context than when the community approved it, which is its own kind of security problem even though technically nothing was 'hacked.' So my execute function always has four checks in this order: does this proposal exist, has the delay actually elapsed, are we still within the grace window, and has it not already been executed — and only after all four pass do I flip the executed flag and make the external call. I'd also flag in review that the external call's success needs to be checked and reverted on failure, otherwise you get a 'successfully executed' proposal that silently did nothing.
commonMistakes: Doesn't track or enforce an eta (delay) before allowing execution
Omits an upper-bound grace period, allowing stale proposals to execute indefinitely later
Sets the executed flag after the external call rather than before, creating a reentrancy window
Doesn't check the external call's return value, silently 'succeeding' on a failed execution
keyPoints: Tracks eta, executed flag, target, and data per proposal
Enforces the delay (eta) correctly before allowing execution
Includes a grace period upper bound on execution
Sets executed flag before the external call and checks its return value

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly enforces delay and grace period
