questions.title: Writing a Foundry Fuzz Test for an AMM Invariant
questions.prompt: Write a Foundry fuzz test that checks a constant-product AMM's `k` value never decreases across a swap (accounting for fees), using random swap amounts as fuzz inputs.
questions.modelAnswer: The test needs to use Foundry's `bound()` (or `vm.assume`) to constrain the fuzzer's randomly generated amountIn into a realistic, non-degenerate range — an unbounded uint256 will mostly generate values that overflow or are economically meaningless, wasting fuzz runs on cases that teach nothing. It captures reserves and computes k before the swap, executes the swap with a real token mint/approve/swap sequence so the test exercises the actual contract path (not a mocked shortcut), then recomputes k after and asserts k after is greater than or equal to k before. The 'greater than or equal' rather than strictly equal matters because a correctly-feed AMM should see k increase slightly on every swap (the fee accrues to the pool, growing reserves beyond what the pure constant-product formula would produce), so a test asserting strict equality would actually be wrong, while assertGe correctly captures the real invariant: the swap should never leave the pool in a worse position than before, ever, for any valid input the fuzzer throws at it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that matters most here is the bound() call — if I let the fuzzer generate a truly unconstrained uint256 for amountIn, the overwhelming majority of runs either overflow somewhere in the math or are so large or small they're not testing anything realistic, so I always constrain the input range to something that reflects real-world swap sizes relative to the pool's reserves. I deliberately go through the real mint-approve-swap path rather than calling some internal shortcut, because fuzzing against a mocked path tells me nothing about the actual deployed contract's behavior. The assertion is assertGe, not assertEq, and that's not a minor detail — if this test asserted k stays exactly equal, it would fail on every single correctly-behaving swap, because the fee is supposed to grow k slightly over time; getting that assertion direction wrong is a classic mistake that either produces false failures or, worse, gets 'fixed' by weakening the test until it stops catching real bugs. What I like about this particular invariant is that it's one of the simplest, highest-signal properties you can fuzz for an AMM — if k ever decreases after a swap, something in the fee or reserve-update math is fundamentally broken, and this test will catch that across a huge range of inputs the author never would have thought to write by hand.
commonMistakes: Uses an unconstrained fuzz input without bound()/vm.assume, wasting runs on degenerate values
Tests against a mocked/internal shortcut rather than the real swap path
Asserts k stays exactly equal (assertEq) instead of non-decreasing (assertGe), fighting the fee mechanism
Doesn't capture reserves/k both before and after the swap correctly
keyPoints: Correctly bounds the fuzz input to a realistic range
Exercises the real swap path, not a mock
Uses the correct non-decreasing (assertGe) invariant direction
Explains why k should grow slightly due to fees, not stay exactly constant

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, realistic bounding of fuzz input

questions.title: Writing a Foundry Invariant Test Suite for a Lending Pool
questions.prompt: Design a Foundry invariant test for a lending pool that checks the protocol is always solvent: total collateral value must always be able to cover total debt, across arbitrary sequences of deposit/borrow/repay/liquidate calls. Describe the handler setup and the invariant assertion.
questions.modelAnswer: The handler contract wraps each real user action (deposit, borrow, repay, liquidate) behind a function Foundry's invariant engine can call in arbitrary sequence and with arbitrary actors, with each function internally bounding its inputs to valid ranges (you can't borrow against collateral you don't have, can't repay more than your debt) so the fuzzer explores realistic-but-adversarial sequences rather than wasting runs on calls that would revert for trivial reasons. The invariant assertion itself — total collateral value (priced through the oracle) must be greater than or equal to total debt value — is checked after every single call in every sequence the invariant engine generates, which is fundamentally different from a unit test checking one specific sequence; it's asking 'no matter what valid sequence of actions real users could ever take, does the protocol stay solvent' across potentially thousands of generated call sequences of varying length and actor combinations. If this invariant ever breaks, Foundry will shrink the failing sequence down to the minimal reproduction, which is enormously more useful for debugging than a hand-written test that happened to catch the same bug by luck.
questions.professionalAnswer: The handler is the piece that takes the most care to get right, because a badly-written handler either reverts constantly on invalid inputs — wasting the fuzzer's entire budget on calls that can never succeed — or it's too permissive and lets the fuzzer generate calls no real actor could actually make, which means you're testing a scenario that isn't real. I bound each handler function to the valid action space: deposit tracks what the acting address actually could deposit, borrow respects the collateral factor so it doesn't even attempt an obviously-invalid borrow, liquidate only fires against targets that are actually unhealthy. Once that's set up, the invariant itself is simple to state but powerful to check: total collateral value has to cover total debt value, always, after every single call in every sequence Foundry generates. What makes this worth the setup effort is that it's checking something a hand-written unit test suite structurally can't — not 'does this one specific sequence of five calls preserve solvency' but 'is there any sequence, out of a huge randomly explored space, that breaks solvency.' And when it does find a break, Foundry's shrinking gives you close to the minimal reproduction case instead of a thousand-call trace you'd have to manually dig through, which is the detail that makes this actually usable day to day instead of just theoretically nice.
commonMistakes: Writes handler functions that constantly revert on invalid inputs, wasting fuzz budget
Doesn't bound handler inputs to the realistic/valid action space, testing unrealistic scenarios
Checks the invariant only once at the end rather than after every call in the sequence
Uses an incorrect or incomplete solvency formula (ignoring price/oracle valuation)
keyPoints: Correctly designs bounded handler functions for each real user action
States a correct, meaningful system-wide solvency invariant
Explains that the invariant is checked across arbitrary generated call sequences
Understands the value of Foundry's failure-shrinking for debugging

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct handler design and input bounding
Explains invariant testing's value over unit tests

questions.title: Writing a Fork Test Against Live Mainnet State
questions.prompt: Describe/write a Foundry fork test that verifies your new contract correctly integrates with a real, already-deployed mainnet protocol (e.g. a real price oracle or a real liquidity pool), rather than a mock. What does forking actually buy you that mocking doesn't?
questions.modelAnswer: Forking spins up a local test environment that's a real snapshot of mainnet state at a specific block, so the test's contract calls out to the actual deployed oracle, the actual deployed token contract, the actual deployed pool — not a hand-written stand-in that only behaves the way the test author assumed it would. This matters because mocks encode the author's beliefs about how a dependency behaves, and if those beliefs are wrong (a function returns data in a different decimal scale than assumed, a real pool has fees baked in a way the mock didn't replicate, an integration point reverts under a condition the author didn't think to mock), the mock-based test passes while the real integration is broken, and that gap only surfaces in production. A fork test forces the integration to prove itself against the real deployed bytecode and real current state, catching decimal mismatches, unexpected revert conditions, and interface assumptions that don't actually hold, which is a category of bug unit tests against mocks are structurally unable to find no matter how thorough the mocking is.
questions.professionalAnswer: What forking buys you is honesty about what you're actually testing against. A mock is only as good as the author's model of how the real contract behaves, and I've seen plenty of integration bugs that were invisible against a mock because the mock quietly encoded the same wrong assumption the integration code made — wrong decimal scaling is the one I see most often, where an oracle test mock returns a price in 1e18 and the real oracle actually returns 1e8, and everything passes against the mock while the real integration would be off by ten orders of magnitude. Forking at a pinned block means my test is calling the actual deployed oracle contract, with its actual deployed logic and actual current state, so if my integration code has a wrong assumption about decimals, return format, or revert conditions, the fork test fails against the real thing instead of passing against a fiction. I always pin the fork to a specific block rather than 'latest,' both for reproducibility — I want the same test to produce the same result every run — and because pinning lets me specifically pick a block where I know certain real-world conditions exist, like a specific price level I want to test my liquidation logic against.
commonMistakes: Doesn't pin the fork to a specific block, making the test non-reproducible
Tests only against a mock, missing decimal/interface/behavior mismatches a real dependency would expose
Doesn't use a real deployed contract address for the dependency being tested against
Fails to explain concretely what category of bug fork testing catches that mocking can't
keyPoints: Pins the fork to a specific block for reproducibility
Tests against the real deployed dependency contract, not a mock
Explains the decimal/interface/behavior-mismatch bug category fork testing uniquely catches
Gives a concrete comparison between mock-based and fork-based test outcomes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct fork test setup (pinned block, real contract)
Correctly explains what forking catches that mocking misses

questions.title: Setting Up Gas Snapshot Testing to Catch Regressions
questions.prompt: Describe how you'd set up Foundry gas snapshot testing in CI to catch gas regressions before merge, and walk through what you'd do when a snapshot diff shows a function's gas cost increased by 40%.
questions.modelAnswer: Setting this up means committing a `.gas-snapshot` file generated by `forge snapshot`, then running `forge snapshot --check` as a required CI step on every pull request, which fails the build if any test's measured gas usage differs from the committed snapshot — forcing gas changes to be an explicit, reviewed decision rather than an invisible side effect of some unrelated refactor. When a diff shows a 40% increase on some function, the response isn't to just regenerate the snapshot and move on; it's to treat that as a signal requiring investigation first — was this an intentional tradeoff (added a necessary safety check that costs gas, in exchange for security), or is it an accidental regression (a loop that got less efficient, a redundant storage read introduced by a refactor, an accidental removal of a gas-saving pattern)? Only after identifying the actual cause and confirming the increase is either justified or has been fixed should the snapshot be regenerated and committed as part of that specific, reviewed pull request, with the reasoning for any accepted increase documented in the PR description so future readers understand why the baseline moved.
questions.professionalAnswer: The setup itself is mechanical — commit the snapshot file, run `forge snapshot --check` as a required CI gate, and now any gas change on any tested function has to show up as an explicit diff in the PR rather than sneaking in unnoticed. The part that actually matters is what I do when that gate fails. A 40% jump on one function is not something I'd just shrug off and regenerate the snapshot to make the build pass — that's exactly the kind of change that deserves five minutes of 'why did this happen' before I decide what to do about it. Sometimes the answer is legitimate: someone added a necessary access-control check or a new safety invariant, and the gas cost is the honest price of that safety. Sometimes it's an accident — a refactor introduced an extra SLOAD inside a loop, or someone accidentally reverted a packed-storage optimization. I treat the investigation as mandatory before touching the snapshot file, and if the increase is accepted, I want that reasoning written down in the PR, not just a silently updated baseline, because six months later nobody's going to remember why gas went up unless it's documented right where the change happened.
commonMistakes: Regenerates the snapshot automatically on failure without investigating the cause first
Doesn't gate CI on `forge snapshot --check`, making the snapshot informational rather than enforced
Treats every gas increase as unacceptable, even when it's a justified safety tradeoff
Doesn't document the reasoning when an increase is accepted
keyPoints: Correctly describes committing and CI-gating the gas snapshot
Treats a gas regression as requiring investigation, not automatic snapshot regeneration
Distinguishes justified tradeoffs from accidental regressions
Documents accepted increases for future readers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound investigation process for a regression

questions.title: Building a GitHub Actions Pipeline for a Foundry Project
questions.prompt: Write (or describe precisely) a GitHub Actions workflow for a Foundry smart contract repo that runs on every pull request: build, unit tests, fuzz/invariant tests, and static analysis — gating the merge on all of them passing.
questions.code:
name: ci
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { submodules: recursive }
      - uses: foundry-rs/foundry-toolchain@v1
      - run: forge build --sizes
      - run: forge test -vvv
      - run: forge snapshot --check
      - name: slither
        uses: crytic/slither-action@v0.4.0
        with: { fail-on: high }
questions.modelAnswer: The workflow needs to trigger on pull_request, check out the repo including submodules (Foundry projects commonly vendor dependencies like forge-std as git submodules, and forgetting `submodules: recursive` is a common setup bug that breaks the build silently in CI even though it works locally), install the Foundry toolchain, then run forge build to catch compilation errors, forge test (including the fuzz and invariant tests, since Foundry runs all test types through the same `forge test` command) to catch logic failures, a gas snapshot check to catch unreviewed gas regressions, and a static analysis step (Slither or Mythril) configured to fail the build on high-severity findings. Every one of these steps needs to be a required status check in the repository's branch protection settings, not just a green checkmark that's informational — a CI pipeline that runs these checks but doesn't actually block merge on their failure provides a false sense of safety, since a determined or rushed contributor can merge past a red check if it isn't enforced as a required gate.
questions.professionalAnswer: The workflow structure itself is fairly standard — checkout with submodules, install the Foundry toolchain, build, test, snapshot check, static analysis — but the detail that trips people up most is forgetting `submodules: recursive` on checkout, because Foundry projects almost always pull in forge-std and other libraries as git submodules, and a CI runner that doesn't pull those in will fail in a confusing way that has nothing to do with your actual code. I run the fuzz and invariant tests through the same `forge test` invocation as the unit tests, since Foundry treats them uniformly, but I make sure the CI config gives them enough runs to be meaningful rather than the fast default meant for local iteration. The static analysis step — Slither in my case — I configure to fail the build on high-severity findings specifically, not everything, because Slither's lower-severity output has enough noise that gating on every finding trains people to ignore the tool entirely. The step I'd never skip explaining in an interview is that none of this matters unless these checks are configured as required status checks in branch protection — I've seen teams build a thorough CI pipeline and then discover six months later that a few PRs got merged with a red X because the checks were never actually required, just displayed.
commonMistakes: Forgets `submodules: recursive` on checkout, breaking Foundry projects that vendor dependencies as submodules
Doesn't include the gas snapshot check or static analysis step in the pipeline
Configures static analysis to fail on every finding, creating noise that trains people to ignore it
Doesn't make the CI checks required status checks in branch protection, leaving them informational only
keyPoints: Includes submodule checkout correctly
Runs build, full test suite (including fuzz/invariant), snapshot check, and static analysis
Configures static analysis severity threshold sensibly
Notes the need for required branch protection status checks, not just a running pipeline

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the submodule checkout gotcha
Explains required status checks / branch protection enforcement

questions.title: Running Slither and Mythril in CI and Triaging Findings
questions.prompt: Describe how you'd wire Slither and Mythril into a CI pipeline for a Solidity repo, and how you'd triage their findings — both tools will report things that aren't real bugs. How do you avoid the team learning to ignore the tooling?
questions.code:
# Slither — fast, pattern-based static analysis
slither . --exclude-dependencies --filter-paths "lib/|test/" --fail-high

# Mythril — slower, symbolic execution; run on a schedule, not every PR
myth analyze src/Vault.sol --execution-timeout 120
questions.modelAnswer: Slither is fast enough to run on every pull request and should be configured to exclude vendored dependencies and test files (otherwise it reports on code the team doesn't own or control, generating noise), filtered to fail the build only on high-severity findings in CI while lower-severity findings get surfaced as PR comments for awareness without blocking merge. Mythril's symbolic execution is significantly slower and more resource-intensive, so running it on every PR is usually impractical; it's better scheduled (nightly or on merge to main) rather than gating every PR, trading immediacy for not slowing down every contributor's feedback loop. Triage for both tools requires maintaining a documented suppression/allowlist for confirmed false positives — with a written justification for each suppression, reviewed periodically — rather than either blocking every finding (which trains the team to view the tool as noise and eventually ignore or routinely dismiss its output) or suppressing broadly (which risks hiding a real finding under an overly wide filter). The actual goal is making true positives rare and high-signal enough that when something does fire, people take it seriously instead of reflexively dismissing it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Slither is cheap enough to run on every single PR, but only if it's configured right — exclude vendored dependencies and test directories from the start, or you'll spend your first week drowning in findings about code your team doesn't even own. I gate CI on high-severity Slither findings specifically, and let medium/low severity show up as PR comments that don't block merge, because gating on everything just trains people to click past red Xs. Mythril is a different story — symbolic execution is slow, and if I tried to run it on every PR, I'd be adding minutes to every contributor's feedback loop for a tool that's more valuable run less frequently but more thoroughly, so I schedule it nightly or on merges to main instead. The triage question is really the important one: both tools throw false positives, and the wrong response in either direction burns trust in the tooling — if you block merge on every single finding including obvious false positives, people start treating the tool as an annoyance to route around; if you suppress too liberally, you risk burying a real finding under a broad filter nobody re-examines. What I actually do is keep a small, documented suppression list with a one-line justification per suppressed finding, reviewed during periodic security check-ins, so the list stays intentional and small rather than becoming a dumping ground that quietly grows until the tool's output is meaningless.
commonMistakes: Runs Mythril on every PR, slowing feedback loops unnecessarily given its cost
Doesn't exclude vendored dependencies/test files from Slither, generating excessive noise
Gates merge on every finding regardless of severity, training the team to ignore the tool
Suppresses findings broadly/undocumented rather than with a reviewed, justified allowlist
keyPoints: Correctly scopes Slither for fast, every-PR execution with sensible exclusions
Schedules Mythril less frequently given its cost
Gates CI on severity-appropriate thresholds, not every finding
Maintains a documented, periodically reviewed suppression list

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct CI integration strategy for both tools

questions.title: Writing a Multisig-Controlled Deployment Script
questions.prompt: Write (or describe precisely) a Foundry deployment script that deploys a contract and transfers ownership/admin control to a multisig as part of the same scripted deployment, rather than as a manual follow-up step.
questions.modelAnswer: The script should read the target multisig address from an environment variable rather than hardcoding it, so the same script can be reused across testnets and mainnet with different multisig addresses without code changes. It deploys the contract while still broadcasting from the deployer's key, immediately calls transferOwnership (or the equivalent admin-transfer function) to hand control to the multisig within the same script execution, and then verifies the transfer actually succeeded by reading back the owner and asserting it matches the intended multisig before the script completes — this verification step matters because a deployment script that assumes a state-changing call succeeded without checking can leave a contract owned by the deployer's single key indefinitely if that call silently failed or was skipped. The goal of doing this in one atomic script rather than as a manual follow-up is specifically to eliminate the dangerous window where a deployed contract sits controlled by a single deployer key before someone remembers to manually run the ownership transfer — that gap, even if brief, is exactly when a compromised or careless deployer key could do real damage.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'm most deliberate about in this script is that ownership transfer isn't a 'next step we'll do after deployment' — it happens inside the same script, same transaction broadcast, so there's no window where this contract exists on-chain controlled by a single deployer key waiting for someone to remember to hand it off. I pull the multisig address from an environment variable specifically so this script is reusable across environments without anyone having to remember to edit a hardcoded address before a mainnet run, which is exactly the kind of manual step that gets forgotten under deployment-day pressure. After calling transferOwnership, I don't just assume it worked — I read the owner back and assert it actually equals the multisig address before letting the script finish successfully, because I've seen 'the transaction succeeded' get confused with 'the state actually changed the way I expected,' and those aren't always the same thing if there's a subtlety in the ownership logic. If I were extending this for a real production deployment, I'd also want the script to log everything meaningfully — the deployed address, the owner it ended up with — into a deployment artifact file, so there's a durable record of exactly what got deployed and who controls it, rather than relying on someone's memory of console output from deployment day.
commonMistakes: Treats ownership transfer to the multisig as a manual follow-up step rather than part of the atomic deployment script
Hardcodes the multisig address instead of reading it from environment/config
Doesn't verify the ownership transfer actually succeeded before the script completes
Doesn't produce a durable deployment record (addresses, owner) for future reference
keyPoints: Performs ownership transfer within the same deployment script, eliminating the single-key window
Parameterizes the multisig address rather than hardcoding it
Verifies the transfer succeeded before considering deployment complete
Produces a clear deployment record/log

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly performs atomic ownership transfer in the script

questions.title: Scripting a Multi-Chain Deployment With Consistent Addresses
questions.prompt: Describe/write a deployment approach for deploying the same contract to multiple EVM chains (e.g. mainnet, Arbitrum, Base) while keeping deployment addresses consistent and configuration correct per chain.
questions.modelAnswer: Keeping addresses consistent across chains requires deploying via CREATE2 with the same salt and the same contract creation code (including constructor arguments, since they affect the creation code hash) on every chain, which produces the same deployed address deterministically regardless of which chain or which deployer nonce state exists on that chain — CREATE (the default) ties the address to the deployer's account nonce, which will differ across chains with different transaction histories, so CREATE2 is the only reliable way to guarantee identical addresses. Beyond the address itself, each chain typically needs its own configuration — different oracle addresses, different token addresses for the same logical asset, different gas price assumptions — so the deployment script needs a per-chain configuration source (environment variables or a config file keyed by chain ID) rather than one hardcoded set of addresses, and the script should assert the actual deployed address matches the predicted CREATE2 address before proceeding, catching a configuration or bytecode mismatch immediately rather than discovering it later when some other chain's deployment doesn't match. Orchestrating the actual rollout across chains should also be sequential with verification at each step, not fire-and-forget in parallel, so a failure or misconfiguration on an early chain is caught before compounding across the rest.
questions.professionalAnswer: The address-consistency problem has one real solution: CREATE2 with a fixed salt and identical creation code, because CREATE ties your deployed address to the deployer account's nonce, and that nonce history is going to be different on every chain unless you've deployed in lockstep from a brand-new account on each one, which isn't realistic. With CREATE2, the address is a deterministic function of the salt and the creation code hash, so as long as both are identical across chains, the address comes out identical too — and I always include constructor arguments in what I'm treating as 'the creation code' here, because people forget those affect the hash and then wonder why their CREATE2 address differs between a chain with one constructor argument and a chain with a slightly different one. The part that trips people up more than the address math is configuration — each chain usually needs a different oracle address, different token addresses for what's logically the same asset, sometimes different gas assumptions, so I drive that from a per-chain config keyed by chain ID rather than hardcoding anything. And I always script in an assertion that the actual deployed address matches the CREATE2 prediction before moving on — if it doesn't, something about the bytecode or constructor args drifted between chains, and I want to know that on chain two, not after I've already deployed to chain five.
commonMistakes: Uses standard CREATE deployment, which produces different addresses depending on deployer nonce per chain
Doesn't account for constructor arguments affecting the CREATE2 address hash
Hardcodes configuration (oracle/token addresses) instead of driving it per-chain
Deploys to all chains in parallel without verifying each before proceeding to the next
keyPoints: Correctly identifies CREATE2 with fixed salt as the solution for consistent addresses
Understands constructor arguments affect the CREATE2 address
Uses per-chain configuration rather than hardcoded values
Verifies each chain's deployment before proceeding, rather than parallel fire-and-forget

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains CREATE2 for address consistency
Describes a sound sequential verification rollout

questions.title: Building a Resilient On-Chain Event Listener Service
questions.prompt: Write/describe the core structure of an event listener service that reliably processes on-chain events, handles missed blocks after downtime, and avoids duplicate processing on restart.
questions.modelAnswer: The service must persist a checkpoint (the last successfully processed block) to durable storage after each batch, not just in memory, so a restart resumes from where it left off rather than from the current chain head, which would silently skip every event that occurred during the downtime. It should only process up to a 'safe head' — the latest block minus a confirmation buffer — rather than the absolute latest block, to avoid processing events from blocks that might still get reorged out. Each event handler needs to be idempotent, keyed by a unique identifier like (transaction hash, log index), because the service might process the same event twice in edge cases — a crash after processing but before saving the checkpoint, for instance — and idempotent processing (checking if this specific event was already recorded before acting on it) means a duplicate delivery doesn't double-credit a deposit or double-fire a side effect. On restart after downtime, loading the persisted checkpoint and querying events from checkpoint-plus-one through the current safe head in one catch-up pass ensures no events are silently missed, which is the entire point of maintaining a durable checkpoint rather than always starting from 'now.'
questions.professionalAnswer: The three things I never skip building into one of these services, because I've debugged incidents caused by missing each of them: a durable checkpoint, a confirmation buffer, and idempotent processing. The checkpoint has to be saved to a database or persistent store after every successful batch, not kept in memory, because the first time this service restarts after a crash or a deploy, if it starts from 'now' instead of 'where I left off,' every event that happened during the downtime just silently never gets processed — and that's an incredibly quiet failure mode that often isn't noticed until someone asks why a specific deposit never showed up. The confirmation buffer matters because querying right up to the chain's absolute latest block means some of those events might get reorged out moments later, so I always process up to latest-minus-N, not latest itself. Idempotency is the one people most often skip because it feels like belt-and-suspenders until the day it saves you — if the service crashes after processing an event but before saving the checkpoint, on restart it's going to see that event again, and if the handler isn't keyed to detect 'have I already recorded this exact transaction hash and log index,' you get a double-processed deposit or a duplicate notification. None of these three is optional in anything handling real value; they're the difference between a toy script and a production service.
commonMistakes: Keeps the checkpoint only in memory, causing it to restart from 'now' after any crash/restart
Processes right up to the latest block with no confirmation buffer, risking reorg-related bad data
Doesn't make event processing idempotent, risking duplicate processing on retries/restarts
Doesn't persist the checkpoint after every batch, widening the gap that could be lost on crash
keyPoints: Persists the checkpoint durably after each processed batch
Processes only up to a safe head behind a confirmation buffer
Makes event processing idempotent, keyed by a unique event identifier
Correctly resumes from the persisted checkpoint after downtime

lessonLink.label: Review: Building a Simple Event Listener Service

questions.title: Writing a Subgraph Schema and Mapping Handler for Marketplace Sales
questions.prompt: Write a subgraph GraphQL schema entity for an NFT marketplace `Sale` and the mapping handler that populates it from a `Sale` event emitted by the marketplace contract.
questions.modelAnswer: The Sale entity should be marked immutable since a completed sale is a historical fact that never changes after the fact, which lets The Graph optimize storage and querying for that entity type. The id must be unique per event, and the standard pattern is combining the transaction hash with the log index (not just the transaction hash alone, since a single transaction could in principle emit multiple Sale events, and not just the log index alone, since that's only unique within a single transaction) — getting this wrong causes silent data loss where a second event with a colliding id overwrites the first. The mapping handler reads fields directly off the typed event parameters that the subgraph's generated types expose, assigns them to the entity's fields, and calls save() to persist it; critically, the handler should do the minimum necessary work and avoid making additional RPC calls mid-handler wherever possible, since mapping handlers run once per matching event across potentially the entire historical range during indexing, and expensive handlers slow down indexing dramatically or can even cause the subgraph to fall out of sync with the chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I mark Sale as immutable because once a sale happens, it happened — nothing about that record should ever change, and telling The Graph that upfront lets it optimize how it stores and serves that entity. The id is the detail I'd spend the most time explaining, because getting it wrong is a silent bug, not a loud one: if I used just the transaction hash as the id and a single transaction somehow triggered two Sale events, the second write would silently overwrite the first and I'd never see an error, I'd just quietly be missing data. Combining transaction hash with log index is the standard fix because log index disambiguates multiple events within the same transaction. In the handler itself, I keep it as lean as possible — read the typed event params, assign them to entity fields, save — because I think of mapping handlers as running potentially millions of times during a full historical reindex, and anything expensive in there, especially an external call, multiplies that cost across the entire history and can make your subgraph fall meaningfully behind the chain or take hours longer to sync than it should.
commonMistakes: Uses only the transaction hash as the entity id, risking silent overwrites when multiple events occur in one transaction
Doesn't mark a genuinely immutable historical entity as immutable
Makes expensive calls or additional lookups inside the mapping handler, slowing indexing significantly
Doesn't use the typed event parameter accessors correctly
keyPoints: Correctly constructs a unique entity id combining transaction hash and log index
Marks historical/immutable entities as immutable appropriately
Writes a lean, efficient mapping handler
Explains the performance cost of expensive handler logic during historical indexing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct schema design and entity id construction

questions.title: Building a Chainlink Price-Triggered Automation Service
questions.prompt: Write/describe a service (or Chainlink Automation-compatible contract) that triggers an on-chain action when a Chainlink price feed crosses a threshold — e.g. triggering a rebalance when an asset drops 10%. What has to be checked to avoid acting on stale or invalid price data?
questions.modelAnswer: Before acting on any price read from `latestRoundData()`, the contract must check that `updatedAt` is recent enough — comparing block.timestamp minus updatedAt against a defined staleness threshold — because a price feed that stops updating (due to an oracle outage or a chain-specific issue) will keep returning its last reported value indefinitely unless the consumer explicitly checks freshness, and acting on a stale price is functionally the same as acting on a wrong price. It must also check the returned price is positive/sane, since a negative or zero price is clearly invalid and should never be acted on. Critically, performUpkeep needs to re-check the trigger condition independently rather than trusting that checkUpkeep's earlier evaluation still holds, because time has passed between those two calls (checkUpkeep runs off-chain in simulation, performUpkeep executes on-chain later) and the price could have moved back above the threshold in that window — executing a rebalance based on a condition that's no longer actually true would be acting on stale logic even with a fresh price.
questions.professionalAnswer: The staleness check is the one I'd never let a reviewer skip, because a price feed that's stopped updating doesn't throw an error, it just keeps returning whatever it last successfully reported — so if I don't explicitly check how long ago `updatedAt` was relative to now, I can't tell the difference between 'the price genuinely hasn't moved' and 'this feed broke three hours ago and nobody's trading against it anymore.' I also sanity-check the price is positive, since a zero or negative value from a misbehaving feed shouldn't ever be treated as real data. The detail I'd specifically call out in a review of someone else's Automation-compatible contract is that performUpkeep has to re-verify the trigger condition itself, not just trust that checkUpkeep already confirmed it — there's a real time gap between when Chainlink's off-chain simulation runs checkUpkeep and when performUpkeep actually lands on-chain, and if the price recovered above the threshold in that window, executing the rebalance anyway means acting on a condition that's already stopped being true. I think of checkUpkeep as 'is it worth trying' and performUpkeep as needing its own independent, fresh confirmation that the thing it's about to do is still the right thing to do.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check price feed staleness via `updatedAt`, risking acting on an outage's last stale value
Doesn't validate the price is positive/sane before acting on it
Trusts checkUpkeep's evaluation without re-verifying the condition inside performUpkeep
Doesn't account for the time gap between checkUpkeep simulation and performUpkeep execution
keyPoints: Correctly checks price feed staleness via updatedAt
Validates price sanity before acting
Re-verifies the trigger condition independently inside performUpkeep
Explains the checkUpkeep/performUpkeep time-gap risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct staleness and sanity checks on price data

questions.title: Implementing Server-Side Sign-In With Ethereum Verification
questions.prompt: Write/describe the server-side logic for verifying a Sign-In With Ethereum (SIWE) message and signature, including the specific checks beyond signature validity that prevent replay and domain-binding attacks.
questions.modelAnswer: Beyond checking that the signature cryptographically matches the claimed address over the exact signed message, the server must verify the nonce embedded in the SIWE message matches a server-issued, single-use nonce that gets invalidated immediately after successful verification — without this, a captured valid signature could be replayed indefinitely to authenticate again, since signature validity alone doesn't expire. It must also check the domain field in the message matches the server's own expected domain, because without domain binding, a signature a user created for one site could be captured and replayed against a different site impersonating the same user (a phishing site could present a SIWE request with its own domain, capture the signature, and replay it elsewhere if domain weren't checked server-side). It should check the expirationTime field if present and reject expired messages, since a long-lived signature increases the window an attacker who somehow intercepts it has to use it. The nonce should be consumed (marked used) atomically with verification success, not just generated and left reusable, closing the replay window completely rather than relying on the client to not resend it.
questions.professionalAnswer: Signature validity alone tells you the private key for that address signed exactly this message — it doesn't tell you this is a fresh login attempt and not a replay of an old captured one, which is exactly why the nonce check matters. I generate a single-use nonce server-side when the login flow starts, embed the expectation that the SIWE message will include it, and the moment verification succeeds, I consume that nonce in the same operation so it can never be used again — if I generated it but didn't tie consumption to successful verification, there'd be a window where the same signed message could be replayed twice. Domain binding is the check I'd specifically flag to a junior engineer as easy to forget and dangerous to skip: SIWE messages include the domain the user believes they're signing in to, and if my server doesn't verify that matches my actual domain, a phishing site could present its own SIWE challenge, capture a valid signature from an unsuspecting user, and replay that exact signature against my real site, and the signature itself would still verify correctly — it's cryptographically valid, it's just valid for the wrong context. Expiration is the belt-and-suspenders layer on top — even with nonce and domain checks right, I don't want a signed message theoretically usable six months from now if something about the nonce-consumption logic ever has a bug.
commonMistakes: Checks signature validity only, without verifying a server-issued single-use nonce
Doesn't check the domain field, leaving the login vulnerable to cross-site signature replay
Generates a nonce but doesn't atomically consume it on successful verification, leaving a replay window
Ignores expirationTime, allowing indefinitely valid signed messages
keyPoints: Verifies a server-issued, single-use nonce as part of the message
Checks domain binding to prevent cross-site signature replay
Checks message expiration
Atomically consumes the nonce on successful verification

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements nonce verification and single-use consumption

questions.title: Managing Nonces and Gas Estimation for a High-Throughput Transaction Sender
questions.prompt: Write/describe the core logic for a backend service that needs to send many transactions from a single hot wallet in quick succession without nonce collisions or stuck transactions. How do you handle gas estimation and nonce management under this load?
questions.modelAnswer: The core problem is that nonce assignment must be serialized even though requests to send transactions may arrive concurrently, because two transactions sent with the same nonce race and only one confirms, silently dropping the other; the fix is maintaining an in-process nonce counter (seeded from the 'pending' count, not just 'latest', so already-broadcast-but-unconfirmed transactions are accounted for) and incrementing it atomically under a mutex or queue so concurrent send requests each get a unique, sequential nonce with no gaps or collisions. Gas estimation under load needs headroom above the current network fee estimate (bumping the suggested maxFeePerGas/maxPriorityFeePerGas by some margin) because fee estimates can be stale by the time the transaction actually gets broadcast and included, and underpricing risks the transaction sitting unconfirmed indefinitely, which is especially dangerous for nonce-ordered sending since a stuck low-nonce transaction blocks every higher-nonce transaction from that same account from confirming, even if they're individually well-priced. A stuck-transaction watcher that detects a transaction hasn't confirmed within an expected window and rebroadcasts it at a higher fee using the exact same nonce (a proper fee-bump/replacement, not a new transaction with a new nonce) is necessary to unblock the queue without creating a second, conflicting transaction at a different nonce for the same intended action.
questions.professionalAnswer: The failure I've actually debugged here is the classic one: two requests to send a transaction come in close together, both read the wallet's current nonce independently, both send with the same nonce, and one of them just silently vanishes from the mempool while the other confirms — nobody gets an error, the second transaction just never happens, and that's a brutal thing to track down after the fact. So nonce assignment has to be serialized, not read fresh per request — I keep an in-memory counter seeded from the pending nonce count, not just the latest confirmed one, specifically because 'latest' ignores transactions I've already broadcast but that haven't confirmed yet, and increment that counter atomically under a lock so every concurrent send gets a unique nonce with no gaps. On gas, I always pad the suggested fee by a meaningful margin, because if I send at the bare minimum estimate and network conditions tick up even slightly before inclusion, that transaction sits stuck — and because nonces are strictly ordered per account, one stuck low-nonce transaction jams every single higher-nonce transaction behind it, even perfectly healthy ones. The piece I make sure exists before this goes anywhere near production is a watcher that notices a transaction hasn't confirmed in a reasonable window and rebroadcasts it at a bumped fee using the exact same nonce — a true replacement, not a new transaction with a fresh nonce, because sending a second transaction at a different nonce doesn't unblock the stuck one, it just adds another transaction waiting behind it.
commonMistakes: Reads the current nonce fresh per request without serialization, risking nonce collisions under concurrency
Seeds the nonce counter from 'latest' confirmed count rather than 'pending', ignoring already-broadcast transactions
Underpads gas fee estimates, risking stuck transactions that block the entire nonce queue
Rebroadcasts a stuck transaction as a brand-new transaction with a different nonce instead of a true fee-bumped replacement
keyPoints: Serializes nonce assignment to avoid collisions under concurrent sends
Seeds the nonce counter from pending, not just latest confirmed
Pads gas fee estimates with margin to reduce stuck-transaction risk
Implements a true same-nonce fee-bump replacement for stuck transactions

questions.title: LPs Are Complaining Their Pool Position Is Worth Less Than Expected
questions.prompt: Several liquidity providers in your constant-product pool are complaining their withdrawn value is noticeably less than what they deposited, even though they earned fees the whole time. Walk through how you'd investigate whether this is a bug or expected impermanent loss, and how you'd communicate the answer either way.
questions.modelAnswer: The first investigative step is pulling the actual price ratio of the pool's two assets at deposit time versus at withdrawal time — if there's been meaningful price divergence between the two assets over that window, some IL is mathematically expected and isn't a bug at all, and the investigation should compute the expected IL for that specific price move and compare it against what the LP actually experienced. If the LP's actual loss materially exceeds the IL the math predicts for that price move, that's the signal something else is wrong — a fee accounting bug, a reserve-update error, or a pool-specific issue (like a fee-on-transfer token behaving unexpectedly within the AMM's accounting) — and that requires auditing the contract's reserve and fee-distribution logic against the specific LP's deposit/withdrawal transactions. If the numbers line up with expected IL, the right response isn't to dismiss the complaint but to walk the LP through the actual math transparently — show them the price move, show them the expected IL calculation, and acknowledge that fees earned partially offset but didn't fully cover it — because LPs who don't understand IL going in are the ones most likely to feel misled, and a clear, honest explanation preserves trust even when the news is 'this was expected, not a bug.'
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I even open the contract code, I pull up the pool's price history and check how far the two assets actually moved apart between this LP's deposit and withdrawal, because that number tells me immediately whether I'm hunting for a bug or explaining expected behavior. I compute what IL should be for that exact move and stack it against what the LP says they actually lost. If those two numbers are in the same neighborhood, I'm not chasing a bug — I'm having an uncomfortable but honest conversation with an LP who didn't fully understand what they signed up for, and I'd rather walk them through the real math with real numbers than let them think something's broken. If their actual loss is noticeably worse than what the IL formula predicts, now I'm suspicious of the contract itself, and the first place I look is fee accounting — am I crediting fees correctly per LP share, is there a token in this pool with fee-on-transfer or rebasing behavior the AMM wasn't built to handle. I've seen that exact thing happen — a pool paired against a fee-on-transfer token where the AMM's reserve bookkeeping quietly drifted from on-chain reality over time, and every LP in that pool was losing more than IL alone would predict, which is a real, fixable bug, not a misunderstanding.
commonMistakes: Assumes it's a bug without first checking whether the price move explains the loss as expected IL
Assumes it's expected IL without verifying the fee/reserve accounting actually matches
Dismisses the complaint without walking the LP through concrete numbers
Doesn't check for pool-specific issues like non-standard token behavior (fee-on-transfer, rebasing)
keyPoints: Computes expected IL for the actual price move before concluding anything
Compares actual loss against expected IL to determine bug vs. expected behavior
Investigates fee/reserve accounting if the loss exceeds expected IL
Communicates the finding transparently to the LP with concrete numbers either way

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound investigative process distinguishing bug from expected IL
Correctly checks fee/reserve accounting as a bug hypothesis
Sound communication approach to the LP

questions.title: The Liquidation Engine Stalled During a Market Crash
questions.prompt: During a sharp market drop, your lending protocol's liquidation engine failed to liquidate a large number of underwater positions in time, and the protocol is now facing bad debt. Walk through how you'd diagnose what actually failed and what you'd fix before the next volatility event.
questions.modelAnswer: The diagnosis starts by checking the oracle's update history during the crash window — if the price feed lagged or didn't update frequently enough during the fast move, positions that were actually underwater on the real market price may not have crossed the on-chain liquidation threshold until much later, which looks identical to 'nobody liquidated' but is actually 'the system didn't know yet.' If the oracle was fine, the next check is liquidator transaction history during the window — were liquidation transactions submitted and failing, or not submitted at all? Failing transactions during a gas spike point to liquidation bonuses that weren't large enough to be profitable at the elevated gas prices of a congested network, meaning the economic incentive broke down exactly when it was needed most. If liquidations simply weren't attempted, that may point to a lack of independent liquidator diversity — if the protocol relied on too few liquidator bots or kept them informally, a single liquidator's own failure (rate limits, RPC outage, bugs) left the system with no backstop. Fixes going forward should include tail-risk-calibrated liquidation bonuses (not averaged against calm markets), a protocol-run backstop liquidation bot as a last resort, and oracle update frequency/heartbeat guarantees stress-tested against historical crash scenarios, not just normal conditions.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first call isn't to the liquidators, it's to the oracle logs, because I've learned the hard way that 'liquidations didn't happen' and 'the price feed didn't know yet' look identical from the outside but need completely different fixes. I pull the exact update timestamps during the crash window and check whether the feed was keeping pace with how fast the real price was moving — if it lagged, positions that were genuinely underwater in reality weren't yet underwater on-chain, and no liquidator bot in the world could have acted on data that didn't exist yet. If the oracle checks out, I go look at whether liquidation transactions were even submitted during that window, and if they were submitted and failed, that's almost always a gas-economics story — the liquidation bonus was sized for a calm Tuesday, not for a network charging ten times normal gas while everyone's scrambling at once, so liquidators did the math and it just wasn't worth it for them to act. If I find out this protocol was leaning on one or two liquidator bots as its entire safety net, that's the part I'd flag hardest in the postmortem, because a single point of failure in your liquidation backstop is exactly the kind of risk that looks fine for months until the one day it really isn't.
commonMistakes: Assumes liquidators simply 'didn't show up' without checking the oracle's update timing first
Doesn't check whether liquidation transactions were attempted and failed versus never attempted
Doesn't connect gas-price spikes during crashes to liquidator profitability
Proposes no concrete fix (tail-risk bonus sizing, backstop liquidator, oracle heartbeat) going forward
keyPoints: Checks oracle update timing/frequency during the crash as a first hypothesis
Distinguishes failed liquidation attempts from liquidations never attempted
Connects gas spikes to broken liquidator economics
Proposes concrete fixes: tail-risk bonus sizing, backstop liquidator, oracle heartbeat stress testing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies plausible root causes (oracle lag, gas economics, liquidator concentration)

questions.title: Post-Mortem: Reconstructing a Flash Loan Exploit
questions.prompt: A protocol you work on was just exploited via a flash loan attack, and funds were drained. Walk through how you'd reconstruct exactly what happened from on-chain data, and what you'd check first to confirm the attack is actually over before resuming operations.
questions.modelAnswer: Reconstruction starts by pulling the exploit transaction itself from a block explorer and decoding every internal call it made, in order — this reveals the exact sequence: which flash loan provider was used, what state was manipulated (a price, a reserve ratio, a governance snapshot), which function on the target protocol was called with the manipulated state, and how the attacker extracted value before repaying the loan, all within that single transaction. Cross-referencing the manipulated state against the target protocol's own logic identifies the specific root-cause flaw (for example, pricing collateral off a manipulable spot price instead of a TWAP or robust oracle). Before resuming operations, the critical first check is whether the vulnerability that enabled this specific attack has actually been fixed and verified — not just that this one attacker's specific transaction pattern was blocked — because flash loan attacks are easily repeated or varied by a different actor exploiting the same underlying flaw the moment the protocol comes back online, and resuming before the root cause is patched (and ideally the fix has been tested against the exact reconstructed attack scenario) risks a second drain within minutes of unpausing. A second check is whether the attacker's drained funds are still movable (not yet bridged/mixed) in case there's a window for a negotiated return or law-enforcement engagement, though this shouldn't delay the technical fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: The very first thing I do is treat the exploit transaction itself as the primary evidence — decode every internal call in order on a block explorer or with a local trace tool, because that transaction tells the complete story: which flash loan source they used, exactly what piece of state they bent out of shape, which function on our side trusted that bent state, and how they walked away with the difference before repaying the loan. Once I can see that chain of calls clearly, the root cause is usually obvious — in my experience it's almost always 'we priced something off a spot value an attacker could move in the same transaction.' The question I'm most paranoid about before anyone talks about unpausing is whether we've actually fixed that root cause or just reacted to this one attacker — blocking a specific address or pattern does nothing, because the moment we come back online, anyone who reads our postmortem or just copies the same trick can run it again against the exact same flaw if it's still there. I want the fix tested against the literal reconstructed attack transaction, replayed against the patched contract, before I'm comfortable calling it resolved. Tracking where the funds moved matters too, but I'm careful not to let that become a distraction from getting the actual patch verified first.
commonMistakes: Focuses only on blocking the attacker's address/transaction pattern rather than fixing the underlying flaw
Doesn't decode the exploit transaction's internal calls to understand the actual mechanism
Resumes operations without verifying the root-cause fix against the reconstructed attack scenario
Doesn't check whether drained funds are still trackable/movable for recovery efforts
keyPoints: Reconstructs the exploit by decoding the transaction's internal call sequence
Identifies the specific root-cause flaw, not just the attacker's address/pattern
Verifies the actual fix against the reconstructed scenario before resuming
Considers fund-tracking/recovery alongside the technical fix

questions.title: A Governance Proposal Passed With Suspiciously Concentrated Voting Power
questions.prompt: A malicious-looking governance proposal just passed with voting power that appeared suddenly and came almost entirely from a handful of addresses that weren't previously active holders. Walk through how you'd investigate whether this was a flash-loan-style governance attack, and what immediate and longer-term steps you'd take.
questions.modelAnswer: The first check is how the voting system sources voting power — if it's based on a balance snapshot taken before proposal creation (the correct design), a flash-loan attack on live balance is already ruled out, and the investigation should instead look at whether tokens were acquired legitimately before the snapshot (perhaps through an OTC deal or accumulation) versus whether the snapshot mechanism itself has a flaw letting post-snapshot balance changes still count. If voting power is instead based on live or near-live balance at vote time, pulling the voting transactions and tracing the source of the voting addresses' token balances (did they borrow via a flash loan or a lending protocol shortly before voting and repay shortly after) would directly confirm the attack mechanism. Immediate steps, if the timelock hasn't yet elapsed on the passed proposal's execution, include using any emergency veto/cancel mechanism the governance system has (if one exists) before the malicious action executes — this is exactly why timelocks matter, since they create the reaction window being used here. Longer-term, the fix is making sure voting power is unambiguously snapshot-based with checkpointed delegation (if it wasn't already), adding or tightening a proposal-to-vote delay, and considering a minimum holding-period requirement before newly-acquired tokens count toward voting power.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I ask before anything else is boring but essential: how does this governance system actually calculate voting power, snapshot-based or live-balance-based? If it's properly snapshotted at proposal creation, I can already rule out a same-block flash-loan attack, and I'd redirect my suspicion toward whether the snapshot mechanism itself has a flaw, or whether someone legitimately accumulated a large position before the snapshot through normal means. If it turns out voting power is live or close to it, I go straight to tracing those suspicious addresses' balance history around the vote — did tokens show up right before voting and vanish right after, which is the signature of a flash loan used to swing a vote. If the malicious proposal hasn't actually executed yet because it's sitting in a timelock, that's genuinely good news — that delay exists for exactly this moment, and I'd want to know immediately whether there's any emergency veto or cancel path available before that window closes. Once the immediate fire is out, the fix going forward is making voting power unambiguously snapshot-based with proper checkpointed delegation if it wasn't already, because I'd rather close this hole permanently than just respond to this one incident.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check how the governance system actually sources voting power before assuming the attack mechanism
Fails to use the timelock's reaction window to attempt a veto/cancel before the proposal executes
Doesn't trace the actual source of the suspicious addresses' token balances
Proposes no concrete longer-term fix (snapshotting, delegation checkpoints, holding periods)
keyPoints: Checks the voting power sourcing mechanism as the first diagnostic step
Traces the suspicious addresses' balance history to confirm or rule out the attack mechanism
Uses the timelock's reaction window for immediate response if the action hasn't executed yet
Proposes concrete longer-term governance hardening

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound diagnostic approach to confirm/rule out the attack mechanism
Correct, timely immediate response using available defenses

questions.title: An Invariant Test Fails in CI but Passes Locally
questions.prompt: Your lending pool's solvency invariant test fails intermittently in CI but you can't reproduce the failure locally, even running the same test command. Walk through how you'd track this down.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check is whether the fuzzer's seed or run configuration differs between local and CI — if CI doesn't pin a fixed seed and runs more fuzz iterations or depth than the local default, it's simply exploring a larger space of call sequences and finding an edge case that local runs with fewer iterations haven't stumbled into yet, which isn't an environment difference at all, just a statistics-of-search-space difference. The fix for reproducing it is running locally with the exact same number of runs/depth CI uses, or better, having CI output the specific failing call sequence (Foundry's shrinker produces this) as an artifact so it can be replayed locally with a fixed seed regardless of iteration count. If the seed and run counts are actually matched and it still only fails in CI, the next suspect is environment-dependent state — a block.timestamp or block.number dependency where CI's fork or anvil instance starts from different initial state than a local one, or a flaky external call to a forked RPC endpoint that times out under CI's network conditions but not locally. The key principle is to capture and persist the exact failing sequence the first time it happens, since an invariant test failure that can't be captured is effectively impossible to fix with confidence — you'd just be guessing at whether a later change actually addressed the root cause.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default assumption with 'fails in CI, passes locally' on a fuzz-driven test is boring: check the run counts before assuming anything mysterious is going on. CI almost always runs more iterations and deeper call sequences than the fast config people use for quick local iteration, so CI is just searching a bigger space and finding something local runs haven't gotten unlucky enough to hit yet — that's not flakiness, that's the test doing its job more thoroughly in CI. The fix is never 'just rerun it until it passes' — I grab the exact failing sequence Foundry's shrinker spits out and save it as a regression test with a fixed seed, so now it reproduces reliably every time regardless of how many fuzz runs anyone configures. If I've matched run counts and seeds exactly and it still only breaks in CI, now I'm actually suspicious of the environment itself — is the CI fork pinned to the same block as local, is there a timestamp dependency that behaves differently, is an RPC call timing out under CI's network conditions. But I check the boring explanation first, because nine times out of ten that's exactly what it is, and chasing exotic environment theories before ruling out 'CI just ran more iterations' wastes a lot of time.
commonMistakes: Assumes it's an 'environment flakiness' issue without first checking fuzz run-count/seed differences
Doesn't capture/persist the specific failing call sequence Foundry's shrinker produces
Tries to fix the failure without being able to reliably reproduce it first
Doesn't consider fork/RPC-dependent flakiness as a real possibility in CI specifically
keyPoints: Checks fuzz seed/run-count configuration differences between local and CI as the first hypothesis
Captures and persists the failing call sequence for reliable reproduction
Considers fork/RPC/timestamp-dependent environment differences as a secondary hypothesis
Insists on reliable reproduction before attempting a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies run-count/seed as the likely first cause

questions.title: Gas Costs Spiked 40% After a Refactor and Nobody Noticed Until Mainnet
questions.prompt: A refactor to a core contract shipped without catching a significant gas regression, and users are now complaining about expensive transactions on mainnet. Walk through how you'd both fix the immediate regression and close the process gap that let it ship unnoticed.
questions.modelAnswer: Fixing the immediate regression requires diffing the refactor's bytecode-level behavior against the prior version function by function to isolate exactly which operations got more expensive — common culprits are a cold SLOAD introduced where a value used to be cached in memory, a loop that got an added iteration or branch, or a struct/storage layout change that increased the number of storage slots touched per call — and then addressing that specific change rather than broadly re-optimizing unrelated code. Closing the process gap requires establishing why this wasn't caught before merge: if gas snapshot testing wasn't in place as a required CI check at all, that's the primary fix — add `forge snapshot --check` as a required, blocking check so any future gas delta is visible and reviewed before merge, not discovered by users after deployment. If gas snapshot testing was in place but this change slipped through anyway, the investigation needs to determine why — was the snapshot not actually gating merge (informational only, not a required status check), did the refactored function lack test coverage so no snapshot even existed for it, or was an increase flagged but approved without real scrutiny. The long-term fix isn't just 'add the tool' but ensuring the tool's output is both comprehensive (every economically significant function has a snapshot) and actually enforced (required, not advisory) going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go function by function comparing the refactor against the previous version's gas profile rather than staring at the whole diff at once, because a 40% jump almost always traces back to one specific change — a value that used to live in memory now reading from storage, a loop that quietly grew a branch, a struct repack that touches more slots than before. Once I've found the specific cause, fixing it is usually straightforward. The part I actually care more about is the process question, because the bug already shipped once and I want to know why. If there was no gas snapshot check gating merges at all, that's the real finding, and the fix is making `forge snapshot --check` a required status check going forward, not an optional nice-to-have. But if a gas snapshot check did exist and this still got through, that's a more interesting problem — maybe the check existed but wasn't actually required in branch protection, maybe this specific function had no test coverage so there was nothing to snapshot in the first place, or maybe someone saw the regression flagged and approved it without really looking. I want an honest answer to which of those happened, because 'add the tool' is the easy fix and 'make sure the tool's output is actually enforced and comprehensive' is the fix that actually prevents a repeat.
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to 'optimize the whole contract' instead of isolating the specific regression first
Fixes the immediate gas issue without investigating why the process let it ship unnoticed
Assumes gas snapshot testing wasn't in place without checking whether it existed but wasn't enforced
Doesn't check for missing snapshot coverage on the specific refactored function
keyPoints: Isolates the specific cause of the gas regression (storage access pattern, loop change, etc.)
Investigates the process gap: missing check, missing enforcement, or missing coverage
Distinguishes a tooling-absence problem from an enforcement problem
Proposes a concrete, enforced fix for the future, not just a one-time patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound diagnostic approach for the specific gas regression
Correctly investigates the process gap that allowed it to ship
Proposes a concrete, enforced long-term fix

questions.title: A Multisig-Controlled Deployment Is Stuck Mid-Rollout
questions.prompt: A scripted multi-step deployment that was supposed to deploy a contract and hand control to a multisig got interrupted partway through — the contract is deployed, but ownership transfer never completed, and one signer is now unreachable. Walk through how you'd safely recover.
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most urgent check is who currently controls the deployed contract — if ownership transfer never completed, the contract is still owned by the deployer's single key, which is itself a live risk that needs addressing with urgency independent of the original rollout plan, since a single key controlling a live contract is exactly the exposure multisig control was meant to eliminate. Before taking any further action, verify the exact current on-chain state (owner address, any pending transactions) rather than assuming the deployment script's last known log is still accurate, since the interruption itself may have left things in a state the script's output doesn't fully reflect. If the deployer key is secure and available, the recovery path is usually to simply re-run (or manually execute) the remaining ownership-transfer step, now pointing at a multisig configuration that accounts for the unreachable signer — which raises the actual blocking issue: if the multisig threshold requires that specific signer and they're unreachable, the transfer can't safely proceed to that exact multisig configuration until either the signer is reached, the threshold is reconfigured (if the multisig contract supports changing owners, which itself may require existing signer consensus), or a decision is made to redeploy the multisig with an adjusted signer set. This is also a good moment to document and fix the gap that allowed a deployment to be considered 'done' while control still sat with a single key — ownership transfer should be an atomic part of deployment, verified before the script is considered successful, exactly to prevent this situation from being possible.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first question I ask isn't 'how do we fix the rollout,' it's 'who controls this contract right now,' because if ownership transfer never finished, the honest answer is a single deployer key, and that's an active exposure I need to treat with urgency on its own, separate from however we eventually get to the multisig. I don't trust the deployment script's last log output to tell me the true current state — I go read the owner address directly on-chain, because the interruption itself might have left things in a slightly different place than the last line the script printed. If the deployer key is secure, getting ownership moved to a multisig is usually simple, except here it isn't, because the multisig's threshold assumes a signer who's currently unreachable, and I'm not going to pretend that's a small detail — if that signer is required to hit threshold, I genuinely can't safely transfer to that exact configuration until either they're reached, the configuration changes, or we deploy an adjusted multisig. Once the immediate situation is resolved, I'd make sure we don't walk away from this without fixing the actual process gap — ownership transfer should never be treated as 'done' separately from deployment, it should be one atomic, verified step, and if it isn't, that's the real lesson from this incident, not just this one stuck rollout.
commonMistakes: Doesn't treat 'contract still owned by a single deployer key' as an urgent, independent risk
Assumes the deployment script's logged state is accurate without re-verifying on-chain
Doesn't address the actual blocker (unreachable required signer) before attempting to proceed
Doesn't flag or fix the underlying process gap that allowed a non-atomic ownership transfer
keyPoints: Treats single-key ownership as an urgent exposure requiring immediate attention
Re-verifies actual on-chain state rather than trusting stale logs
Correctly identifies the unreachable-signer threshold issue as the real blocker
Proposes fixing the non-atomic deployment process going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes the single-key ownership risk
Correctly reasons about the unreachable-signer blocker
Proposes a sound process fix for the future

questions.title: You Just Detected an Active Exploit in Progress — What Do You Check First
questions.prompt: Monitoring alerts you to transactions that look like an active exploit draining funds from your protocol right now. Walk through the first five minutes: what you check, what you decide, and in what order.
questions.modelAnswer: The first action is confirming the alert is real and understanding its scope fast — pulling the specific transaction(s) from a block explorer to see exactly what function was called and what value moved, rather than acting on an alert's summary alone, since a false positive triggering an emergency pause has its own real cost (user-facing disruption, loss of trust) that shouldn't be paid for a non-event. Once confirmed as real, the immediate decision is whether to trigger the protocol's pause mechanism, if one exists — this should be a fast, pre-authorized action (not requiring a fresh multisig round of deliberation under time pressure) specifically because incident response plans should pre-authorize pause-triggering for exactly this scenario, with the harder governance questions (how to fix, how to make users whole) deferred to after the bleeding has stopped. In parallel with or immediately after pausing, the team needs to start tracking where the drained funds are going (which addresses, whether they're moving toward a bridge or mixer, which is relevant for any recovery or law-enforcement engagement) and begin assembling the facts needed for both the technical fix and the first public communication, because a visible exploit without any protocol communication for hours erodes trust independent of the financial loss itself. The order matters: confirm real, then stop the bleeding (pause), then everything else — investigation depth, root-cause analysis, and detailed communication all come after the pause, not before it, because every minute spent fully understanding the exploit before pausing is a minute more value can drain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first ninety seconds are about confirming this is real, not about understanding it fully — I pull the actual transaction off a block explorer and look at what function got called and what moved, because triggering an emergency pause on a false alarm has a real cost too, and I don't want to pay that cost for a non-event. The moment I believe it's real, the decision I make is to pause, immediately, and this is exactly why I push so hard beforehand for pause authority to be pre-approved rather than something that needs a fresh multisig conversation under pressure — every minute spent debating whether to pause is a minute more value draining out the door. Once it's paused, I'm not trying to fully understand the exploit yet, I'm doing two things in parallel: starting to track where the funds are moving in case that matters for recovery later, and getting someone on communications drafting a short, honest acknowledgment, because I've watched protocols go dark during exactly this kind of moment and the silence becomes its own headline. Deep root-cause analysis, the full fix, the detailed postmortem — all of that comes after the bleeding has stopped, never before. The order is non-negotiable in my head: confirm it's real, stop it, then everything else.
commonMistakes: Spends too long fully investigating before triggering an available pause mechanism
Triggers an emergency pause without first confirming the alert represents a real, active exploit
Doesn't address fund tracking in parallel with technical response
Delays any public communication, letting silence compound the trust damage
keyPoints: Confirms the alert is a real exploit before acting, but quickly
Prioritizes triggering the pause mechanism to stop ongoing loss as the first real action
Tracks drained funds in parallel with technical response
