Recognizes that delayed communication compounds damage independent of financial loss

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct prioritization: confirm, then pause, then investigate deeply
Sound reasoning on pre-authorized emergency response
Addresses fund tracking and communication appropriately

questions.title: Your Primary RPC Provider Had an Outage and Your Backend Missed Events
questions.prompt: Your event-listener service's primary RPC provider went down for 40 minutes, and your indexed data is now missing events from that window. Walk through how you'd detect this happened, recover the missing data, and prevent it next time.
questions.modelAnswer: Detecting the gap requires comparing the service's last successfully processed block (its checkpoint) against the chain's actual current head once the provider recovers — a large gap between checkpoint and chain head, or a service that logged repeated request failures during the outage window, is the direct signal, though ideally this is caught by active alerting on 'checkpoint is falling behind chain head' rather than discovered manually after the fact. Recovery is mechanically straightforward if the service was built correctly in the first place: since the checkpoint-based catch-up pattern processes from checkpoint-plus-one through current safe head on every run, simply letting the service resume (now against a working provider) naturally backfills the missed window in its next poll cycle, with no special one-off recovery script needed — this is exactly why durable checkpointing matters, because the recovery path is just 'resume normally.' Prevention for next time means the service shouldn't have had a single point of failure on one RPC provider at all: implementing provider failover (a prioritized list of providers, automatically switching to a secondary when the primary times out or errors repeatedly) means a single provider's 40-minute outage becomes a brief, automatic failover rather than a 40-minute data gap and manual incident. If failover already existed but didn't trigger, the investigation needs to determine why — was the primary returning slow-but-technically-successful responses rather than clean failures, since failover logic that only checks for hard errors can miss a provider that's degraded rather than fully down.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detection signal I'd look for first is simple: how far behind is our checkpoint compared to the chain's current head, and ideally I'm not finding that out manually after the fact, I've got alerting that fires the moment that gap starts growing. The genuinely good news, if the service was built the way I'd build it, is that recovery doesn't need a special script at all — because the service already processes from checkpoint-plus-one up to the current safe head every single cycle, just letting it resume against a healthy provider means it naturally backfills the missed 40 minutes on its own next run. That's the entire payoff of doing durable checkpointing correctly in the first place. What I actually care about after the dust settles is why this became a 40-minute gap instead of a non-event, and the answer is almost certainly that we had one RPC provider as a hard dependency with no failover. I'd fix that going forward with a prioritized provider list and automatic switching on repeated errors or timeouts. And if it turns out failover logic already existed but just didn't trigger, I want to know specifically why — my bet would be the primary was responding slowly but technically successfully rather than cleanly erroring out, and failover logic that only watches for hard failures misses a provider that's degraded instead of fully dead.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check the checkpoint-vs-chain-head gap as the direct detection signal
Writes a special one-off recovery script instead of recognizing the existing checkpoint-catchup logic should handle it automatically
Doesn't propose RPC provider failover as the actual prevention, treating this as a one-time fluke
Doesn't investigate why failover (if it existed) failed to trigger on a degraded-but-not-hard-failing provider
keyPoints: Detects the gap via checkpoint-vs-chain-head comparison or proactive alerting
Recognizes that correct checkpoint-based design allows automatic catch-up without a special recovery script
Proposes RPC provider failover as the real prevention mechanism
Considers degraded-but-not-hard-failing provider behavior as a failover design risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about automatic recovery via existing checkpoint design

questions.title: Your Indexer Shows Deposits That Don't Exist on Mainnet Anymore
questions.prompt: Users are reporting balances in your application that don't match what's actually on-chain, and you suspect a chain reorg wasn't handled correctly by your indexer. Walk through how you'd confirm this and fix the indexed data.
questions.modelAnswer: Confirming the hypothesis means picking one of the affected users' phantom deposits and checking, using the stored transaction hash, whether that transaction actually exists in the current canonical chain — if the transaction hash returns 'not found' or exists but in a different block than what's indexed, that directly confirms the data came from a block that was later reorged out and the indexer never detected or corrected for it. The fix requires first identifying the full scope: finding every indexed record whose source block hash doesn't match what's currently canonical at that height, not just the one reported case, since a reorg that caused one phantom deposit likely caused several other now-invalid records across the same block range. Those invalid records need to be explicitly invalidated or deleted (not just overwritten, which could leave inconsistent downstream aggregates like running balance totals that were calculated including the bad data), and then the correct canonical events for that block range need to be reprocessed and re-indexed properly. Going forward, the actual root-cause fix is in the indexer's design, not a one-time data cleanup: it needs to track block hashes (not just numbers) for everything it's indexed, detect when a previously-indexed block hash no longer matches canonical chain state, and automatically roll back and reprocess affected ranges — this is the correct design pattern that should have existed from the start, and the data cleanup being done now needs to be paired with actually shipping that fix, or the exact same corruption will recur on the next reorg.
questions.professionalAnswer: I never act on a hunch here without proof, so the first thing I do is grab the exact transaction hash behind one reported phantom deposit and check it directly against the current canonical chain — if that hash comes back not found, or shows up in a completely different block than what we indexed, that's definitive confirmation this came from a block that got reorged out and we never noticed. Once I've confirmed the mechanism, I don't just fix the one reported case — a reorg deep enough to cause one phantom deposit almost certainly corrupted other records in that same block range, so I'd scan for every indexed record whose source block hash no longer matches canonical reality. Those records need to be properly invalidated, not just quietly overwritten, because if there's any running balance total that was computed including that bad data, overwriting the source record without fixing the aggregate leaves a second, harder-to-find bug behind. The part I'd stress hardest in the postmortem is that cleaning up this specific data doesn't fix anything long-term — the indexer needs to actually track block hashes, not just numbers, and detect when a previously-indexed hash stops matching canonical state, so it can roll back and reprocess automatically. If we fix the data today and ship the exact same indexer logic tomorrow, we're just scheduling the next version of this same incident.
commonMistakes: Confirms the symptom without tracing a specific transaction hash to definitively prove the reorg hypothesis
Fixes only the reported record without checking for other affected records in the same block range
Overwrites bad data without checking/fixing downstream aggregates that were computed including it
Fixes the data without fixing the indexer's underlying lack of reorg detection, risking recurrence
keyPoints: Confirms the hypothesis by tracing a specific transaction hash against current canonical chain state
Scopes the full extent of affected records, not just the reported one
Correctly invalidates/reprocesses affected data including downstream aggregates
Fixes the indexer's underlying reorg-detection gap to prevent recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly scopes and fixes affected data including aggregates
Addresses the underlying indexer design gap

questions.title: A Subgraph Is Falling Further Behind the Chain Every Day
questions.prompt: Your deployed subgraph's indexed data is increasingly stale — it was a few blocks behind last week and is now hours behind. Walk through how you'd diagnose the cause and what you'd do if the fix requires a full re-index.
questions.modelAnswer: The first diagnostic step is checking the subgraph's sync status and logs for the processing rate per block versus the chain's actual block production rate — if mapping handlers are taking longer per block than new blocks are being produced, the gap will only ever widen, never stabilize, which is the signature of a handler performance problem rather than a transient blip. Common root causes for slow handlers include making external calls (contract calls back to the chain, or HTTP calls) inside a mapping handler, which get executed once per matching event across potentially the entire historical and ongoing event stream and are dramatically more expensive than reading data already available in the event parameters; or an entity design that requires expensive lookups/joins during every handler execution rather than denormalized, cheap-to-write data. Confirming the hypothesis means reviewing the mapping code for exactly these patterns, not just assuming based on symptoms. If the fix requires changing the schema or handler logic in a way that affects historical data (not just going-forward processing), a full re-index is usually unavoidable, since subgraphs generally can't retroactively reinterpret already-indexed history under a new schema without reprocessing from genesis or from a defined starting block; this needs to be planned as a deliberate migration — deploying the fixed subgraph as a new version, letting it fully sync in parallel before cutting application traffic over to it, rather than taking down the only running instance and leaving the application without indexed data during the re-sync window, which could take hours or days depending on the event volume.
questions.professionalAnswer: 'A few blocks behind becoming hours behind' tells me this isn't a blip, it's a structural rate problem — the subgraph is processing each block slower than new blocks are arriving, so the gap mathematically only grows from here, it was never going to fix itself. I'd go straight to the mapping code looking for the two usual suspects: an external call inside a handler — reaching back out to the chain or hitting an HTTP endpoint — which gets paid for on every single matching event across the whole indexing history, or an entity design that needs expensive lookups on every write instead of just storing denormalized data cheaply. Once I find the actual cause, the uncomfortable truth is that if the fix changes schema or handler logic in a way that affects how history gets interpreted, I usually can't just patch it going forward — subgraphs don't retroactively reinterpret already-indexed data, so I'm looking at a real re-index. I wouldn't do that by taking down the only running version and hoping the resync finishes quickly — I'd deploy the fixed version as a new instance, let it fully catch up in parallel while the old one keeps serving traffic, and only cut over once the new one's actually caught up to the chain head, because leaving the application with zero indexed data for however many hours a full resync takes is its own self-inflicted incident.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check whether the handler processing rate is slower than block production rate (confirming a growing-gap problem)
Doesn't check for expensive calls inside mapping handlers as the likely root cause
Doesn't plan the re-index as a parallel-deploy-then-cutover migration, risking application downtime
Assumes the issue is transient/self-resolving rather than diagnosing a structural handler performance problem
keyPoints: Diagnoses a widening gap as a structural handler-performance issue, not a transient blip
Identifies expensive calls/lookups inside mapping handlers as the likely root cause
Recognizes re-indexing requirements when schema/handler logic changes retroactively
Plans a parallel-deploy-then-cutover migration to avoid application downtime

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound diagnostic approach for the widening sync gap
Correctly identifies likely root causes in handler design
Sound migration plan for a required re-index

questions.title: A Chainlink Price Feed Is Returning a Price That Looks Wrong
questions.prompt: Your protocol's price-dependent logic just acted on what looks like an incorrect Chainlink price. Walk through how you'd determine whether this was stale data, a genuine market event, or something else — and what you'd check before concluding the oracle itself is broken.
questions.modelAnswer: The first check is pulling the feed's actual `latestRoundData()` history around the time in question and examining the `updatedAt` timestamps — if the feed hadn't updated in an unusually long time relative to its normal heartbeat, the 'wrong' price might simply be stale, and the real bug is in the consuming contract not checking staleness, not in Chainlink's reporting itself. If the feed was updating on a normal cadence, the next check is comparing that price against other independent sources (other oracle networks, or the asset's actual market price across several exchanges) for the exact same timestamp — if multiple independent sources agree with the 'surprising' price, it may simply reflect a real, fast market move that looked wrong only because it was unexpected, not because anything malfunctioned. If the Chainlink price genuinely diverged from multiple independent sources at the same timestamp, that points to either a problem specific to that feed's underlying data sources, or, in a worst case, some manipulation of whatever markets that specific feed's node operators are aggregating from — this is a much rarer and more serious finding that would warrant direct engagement with Chainlink's team and pausing any logic relying on that specific feed until clarified. The key discipline is working through staleness, then cross-source verification, before ever concluding the oracle network itself is compromised, since the first two explanations are overwhelmingly more common than the third.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep a strict order of operations here because it's so easy to jump to 'the oracle is broken' and waste a day investigating the wrong thing. First I check the feed's own update history — was `updatedAt` recent relative to its normal heartbeat, or had it gone quiet longer than usual, because if it's stale, the bug is in our consuming contract not checking freshness, not in Chainlink's reporting. If the feed was updating normally, I pull up a couple of independent sources — another oracle network, or just the asset's price across a few exchanges, at that exact timestamp — and if they all agree with the number that looked surprising, that's usually just a fast, real market move that felt wrong because nobody expected it, not anything malfunctioning. Only if the Chainlink price genuinely diverges from multiple independent sources at the same moment do I start taking the 'something's actually wrong with this feed' hypothesis seriously, and that's a much bigger deal — that's when I'd be pausing anything that depends on that specific feed and reaching out to Chainlink directly rather than guessing. In my experience staleness and 'it was just a real fast move' account for the overwhelming majority of 'the oracle looks wrong' tickets, and I'd rather rule those out quickly than jump straight to the scariest explanation.
commonMistakes: Jumps to 'the oracle is broken/manipulated' without first checking for simple staleness
Doesn't cross-check against independent price sources before concluding the feed itself is wrong
Doesn't consider that a 'wrong-looking' price might reflect a real, fast market move
Doesn't distinguish a consuming-contract staleness bug from an actual oracle data problem
keyPoints: Checks feed update timestamps for staleness as the first hypothesis
Cross-checks against independent sources before assuming oracle malfunction
Considers that the price may reflect a genuine, fast real-world market move
Reserves 'oracle is compromised/broken' as a last, carefully-verified conclusion

questions.title: Your Gasless Relayer Is Being Drained by Abusive Transactions
questions.prompt: Your protocol sponsors gas for user transactions via a relayer to support gasless UX, and you've noticed the relayer's funds depleting much faster than expected. Walk through how you'd determine if this is organic growth or abuse, and how you'd fix it without breaking the gasless experience for legitimate users.
questions.modelAnswer: Distinguishing organic growth from abuse starts with looking at the distribution of sponsored transactions by originating address — organic growth shows a wide, roughly expected spread across many distinct users doing meaningful actions, while abuse typically shows a small number of addresses generating a disproportionate share of sponsored transactions, often cheap, repetitive, or economically meaningless calls designed purely to drain the sponsor's funds (or to farm some reward the relayer wasn't meant to subsidize at scale). Confirming abuse means examining what those high-volume addresses are actually calling — a pattern of near-identical, low-value transactions from a small address set is a strong signal, especially if it correlates with a farming or airdrop-hunting incentive elsewhere in the ecosystem. The fix needs rate-limiting or cost-capping per address (a maximum number of sponsored transactions per address per time window, or a maximum sponsored gas spend per address) rather than shutting off sponsorship broadly, since broad shutoff breaks the experience for the legitimate majority to punish a small abusive minority. For legitimate high-frequency users who might hit a naive per-address cap, a secondary mechanism — proof of some minimal stake, a reputation/allowlist system, or a small required fee above a certain usage threshold — can distinguish real heavy users from abuse without fully reverting to a bad UX for everyone.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I pull up is the distribution of sponsored transactions by address, because organic growth and abuse look completely different in that shape — organic growth is a broad spread across lots of distinct users, abuse is usually a small handful of addresses accounting for way more volume than they should. If I see that concentration, I go look at what those specific addresses are actually calling, and near-identical, cheap, repetitive calls from a small set of addresses is about as clear a signal as you get, especially if it lines up suspiciously well with some farming or airdrop-hunting incentive happening elsewhere. Once I'm confident it's abuse, I'm deliberate about not overcorrecting — I will not just turn off gasless sponsorship for everyone to punish a handful of bad actors, that breaks the exact experience we built this for in the first place. I'd implement per-address rate limits or a capped sponsored-gas budget instead, targeted specifically at the abuse pattern. The thing I'd make sure not to miss is legitimate power users who might get caught by a naive cap — for those, I'd want some secondary signal, a reputation system, an allowlist, maybe a small fee kicking in above a usage threshold, so real heavy users aren't punished the same as someone farming the relayer for free gas.
commonMistakes: Doesn't distinguish abuse from organic growth via concentration/distribution analysis before reacting
Reacts by disabling gasless sponsorship broadly, breaking UX for legitimate users
Doesn't examine what the high-volume addresses are actually calling to confirm genuine abuse
Proposes no mechanism to distinguish legitimate heavy users from abusive ones going forward
keyPoints: Analyzes transaction distribution/concentration to distinguish abuse from organic growth
Confirms abuse by examining the actual pattern of calls from suspect addresses
Proposes targeted rate-limiting/cost-capping rather than broad shutoff
Proposes a mechanism to accommodate legitimate heavy users without reverting to bad UX

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound diagnostic approach distinguishing abuse from organic growth

questions.title: A Vesting Cliff Unlocked More Tokens Than It Should Have
questions.prompt: A team member reports that a vesting contract just released more tokens to a recipient than the published schedule should have allowed at this date. Walk through how you'd diagnose whether this is a contract bug, a configuration error, or a misunderstanding of the schedule — and how you'd handle the recipient's already-claimed tokens.
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is recomputing, independently and by hand or script against the published schedule's actual parameters (start time, cliff duration, total duration, total amount), exactly how many tokens should be vested and claimable as of the current timestamp — comparing that correct figure against both what the contract reports as claimable and what was actually transferred out tells you immediately whether the bug is in the contract's vesting-math logic, in how the contract was configured/deployed (wrong start timestamp or wrong cliff duration passed to the constructor, which is a configuration error rather than a logic bug), or whether the contract behaved correctly and the complaint stems from a misunderstanding of the schedule's actual terms. If it's a genuine contract logic bug (an off-by-one in a time calculation, an incorrect formula for the linear-vesting portion after the cliff), the contract needs to be identified as unsafe for any other address using the same vesting logic, not just the reported one, since the same bug likely affects every vesting schedule deployed from the same contract or factory. For tokens already claimed in excess of what should have vested, the response depends on whether the contract has any clawback mechanism (most don't, since vesting contracts are usually designed to be trust-minimized and irreversible by design) — if there's no clawback capability, the realistic options are limited to a direct conversation with the recipient about voluntarily returning the excess, or, if the excess is material, treating it as a loss to be absorbed and transparently disclosed, rather than any technical recovery, since you generally can't claw back tokens that have already legitimately left a contract under its own rules.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I believe anyone's claim that 'too many tokens unlocked,' including an internal team member's, I recompute the correct answer myself from the published schedule's actual parameters — start time, cliff length, total duration, total amount — and see exactly what should be claimable right now. Comparing that against what the contract actually released tells me immediately which of three things happened: a real bug in the vesting math, a configuration mistake where someone passed the wrong start timestamp or cliff length at deployment, or the contract did exactly what it was supposed to and someone's just misreading the schedule's actual terms. If it turns out to be a genuine logic bug — an off-by-one somewhere in the linear-vesting calculation is a classic one — my next question isn't 'how do we fix this recipient's issue,' it's 'is every other vesting schedule deployed from this same contract or factory affected,' because it almost certainly is. The hard conversation is what happens to tokens already claimed in excess. I check the contract for any clawback capability first, but honestly, most vesting contracts are deliberately built without one, specifically so recipients can trust the schedule won't be unilaterally changed later — which means if the excess already left the contract, the realistic options are a direct, honest conversation asking for voluntary return, or accepting and transparently disclosing the loss. There usually isn't a clean technical undo once tokens have legitimately left under the contract's own rules.
commonMistakes: Doesn't independently recompute the correct vested amount before assuming a bug exists
Doesn't distinguish a contract logic bug from a deployment/configuration error
Assumes other vesting schedules on the same contract are unaffected without checking
Assumes a clawback is possible without checking whether the contract actually supports one
keyPoints: Independently recomputes the correct vested amount from the schedule's actual parameters
Distinguishes a logic bug from a configuration/deployment error
Checks whether other vesting schedules on the same contract/factory are similarly affected
Realistically assesses recovery options given most vesting contracts have no clawback

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound diagnostic approach distinguishing bug vs. config vs. misunderstanding
Correctly checks for broader impact across other schedules
Realistic assessment of recovery options for already-claimed tokens

questions.title: A Concentrated Liquidity Position Went Out of Range Faster Than Expected
questions.prompt: A sophisticated LP using a concentrated-liquidity pool is asking why their position stopped earning fees much sooner than they modeled. Walk through how you'd investigate whether this is expected range-exit behavior, a pricing/tick calculation bug, or a misunderstanding of how their specific range was set.
questions.modelAnswer: The first step is pulling the actual on-chain price history for the pool over the relevant period and comparing it against the LP's stated range bounds — if the price genuinely moved outside their chosen range, the position correctly stopped earning fees exactly as concentrated liquidity is designed to behave, and the 'bug' is really a gap between the LP's price-volatility assumptions and what actually happened, which is a modeling problem, not a protocol bug. If the price stayed within the LP's intended range per their own description but the position still shows as inactive/non-fee-earning, the next check is verifying the position's actual on-chain tick bounds match what the LP believes they set — a common real cause here is a front-end or script rounding the LP's intended price bounds to the nearest valid tick spacing in a way the LP didn't realize, producing an actual range narrower or offset from what they thought they configured. If the on-chain tick bounds do match the LP's understanding and price genuinely stayed in range, that would point to an actual contract-level tick-crossing or fee-accounting bug, which is a much more serious finding requiring careful review of the swap/fee-accrual logic specifically around tick boundaries — but this should be the last hypothesis checked, after the simpler and far more common explanations (price genuinely exited range, or tick-rounding mismatch) have been ruled out.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by just pulling the actual price history for the pool and laying it next to the range the LP says they set, because the single most common explanation by far is that price genuinely left their range, and the position doing exactly what concentrated liquidity is supposed to do when that happens isn't a bug — it's a gap between what they modeled and what actually happened in the market. If price genuinely stayed inside their described range the whole time and the position is still showing as inactive, now I'm checking something more specific: does the position's actual on-chain tick bounds match what the LP thinks they set. I've seen this exact mismatch before — a front-end rounds the user's intended price bounds to the nearest valid tick spacing, and the LP never realizes their actual on-chain range is narrower or shifted from what they typed in, so their real range exits sooner than their mental model predicted. Only after I've ruled out both of those — genuine range exit and tick-rounding mismatch — would I escalate to actually suspecting a tick-crossing or fee-accrual bug in the contract itself, and that's a much heavier investigation I don't want to open until the two far more common explanations are properly ruled out first.
commonMistakes: Assumes a contract bug before checking whether price simply exited the LP's actual range
Doesn't check for tick-spacing rounding differences between the LP's intended range and the actual on-chain range
Doesn't verify the actual on-chain tick bounds match the LP's stated understanding of their position
Jumps to the most serious hypothesis (contract bug) before ruling out simpler explanations
keyPoints: Compares actual price history against the LP's range bounds as the first check
Checks for tick-spacing rounding differences between intended and actual on-chain range
Verifies on-chain position bounds against the LP's stated understanding
Reserves a contract-bug hypothesis for last, after ruling out simpler explanations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies tick-rounding as a realistic root cause
Appropriately cautious escalation to a contract-bug hypothesis

questions.title: Designing a Full DeFi Lending Protocol End to End
questions.prompt: You're kicking off a capstone-style project to design a complete DeFi lending protocol from scratch — contracts, backend, testing, and deployment. Walk through your end-to-end architecture: the core contracts, how they interact, what off-chain infrastructure supports them, and how you'd sequence the build.
questions.modelAnswer: The core contracts needed are a pool contract (tracking deposits, borrows, and accruing interest via a utilization-based rate model), a price oracle integration (ideally wrapping a decentralized feed like Chainlink rather than reading any single source directly), a liquidation module (computing health factors and executing partial liquidations with an appropriately-sized bonus), and a configuration/admin layer gated by a multisig and timelock for parameters like collateral factors and supported assets. Off-chain, the protocol needs an indexer (subgraph or custom) to serve the front-end's historical and relational queries efficiently, a monitoring service watching protocol health metrics (utilization, aggregate collateralization) and alerting on anomalies, and ideally a backstop liquidation bot ensuring positions get liquidated even if no external liquidator responds in time. Sequencing the build should go: core pool and interest-rate logic first with unit and fuzz tests, then oracle integration and liquidation logic with fork tests against a real deployed oracle, then invariant tests proving system-wide solvency across arbitrary call sequences before any testnet deployment, then testnet deployment with the full off-chain stack (indexer, monitoring) running against it to validate the whole system together, and only then a staged mainnet launch with value caps and a phased rollout, because building and testing contracts in isolation from the off-chain stack that's supposed to monitor and serve them risks discovering integration gaps only after real funds are at stake.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd sketch this as four contract pieces working together — the pool itself handling deposits, borrows, and interest accrual off a utilization curve; an oracle wrapper rather than reading any single price source directly; a liquidation module doing health-factor math and partial liquidations; and an admin layer that's deliberately boring, gated behind a multisig and timelock, because collateral factors and supported-asset lists are exactly the kind of parameter where a single compromised key would be catastrophic. But I wouldn't stop at the contracts, because a lending protocol that's only contracts isn't actually runnable — I need an indexer so the frontend isn't trying to query raw chain state for things like 'show me all my positions,' and a monitoring service watching utilization and aggregate health that pages someone before things go sideways, not after. I'd also want a backstop liquidation bot from day one rather than hoping external liquidators show up reliably. On sequencing, I build and fuzz-test the pool and rate logic first in isolation, then bring in the oracle and liquidation logic with fork tests against the real deployed oracle, then run invariant tests proving solvency holds across arbitrary sequences before I'll even consider a testnet. And testnet isn't just 'deploy the contracts' — I want the whole stack, indexer and monitoring included, running against it together, because the gaps that bite you in production are usually the ones between pieces, not within any single piece tested alone.
commonMistakes: Designs only the contracts without addressing the off-chain indexing/monitoring stack needed to actually run the protocol
Doesn't gate admin/configuration changes behind a multisig and timelock
Sequences testnet/mainnet deployment before invariant testing proves system-wide solvency
Doesn't mention a backstop liquidation mechanism for when external liquidators don't respond
keyPoints: Names the core contract components and how they relate (pool, oracle, liquidation, admin/governance)
Includes necessary off-chain infrastructure (indexer, monitoring, backstop liquidator)
Proposes a sound build sequence ending in staged, capped mainnet launch
Gates admin/configuration behind multisig and timelock

questions.title: Designing an NFT Marketplace End to End
questions.prompt: Design a full NFT marketplace: the contract architecture for listing and settling sales, the indexing layer that lets a front-end browse listings efficiently, and the frontend/wallet integration. What are the key architectural decisions and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The marketplace contract's core decision is whether listings are stored fully on-chain (safer, more gas-expensive, always-authoritative) or signed off-chain and only settled on-chain at purchase time (an order-book pattern where a seller signs a listing message off-chain, and a buyer's transaction verifies that signature and executes the transfer/payment atomically) — the signature-based approach is generally preferred at scale because it avoids the gas cost of writing every listing to chain state, while still being fully trust-minimized since the actual transfer and payment only happen through a verified, on-chain settlement transaction. Royalty handling needs a decision up front: honoring EIP-2981 royalties advisory-style, or embedding royalty payment directly into the settlement function so it can't be bypassed, which matters more if the collection creator cares about enforcement. The indexing layer needs a subgraph (or equivalent) tracking Listing and Sale entities from emitted events, since a front-end browsing 'all active listings for this collection sorted by price' can't practically query that from raw chain state. Frontend/wallet integration needs to handle the off-chain signature flow for listings (prompting the seller to sign a structured message, not a transaction, for gas-free listing creation) and the on-chain transaction flow for actual purchases, with clear UX distinguishing the two so users understand which actions cost gas and which don't.
questions.professionalAnswer: The decision I'd make first, before anything else, is how listings get created — fully on-chain, which is simple and always authoritative but means every single listing costs the seller gas, or signed off-chain and only settled on-chain at purchase time, which is the pattern I'd actually lean toward at any real scale, because it means listing something is free for the seller and the trust-minimization still holds since the actual transfer and payment only happen through a verified on-chain transaction. Royalties are the next explicit call — am I just honoring EIP-2981 as advisory and trusting marketplaces to pay it, or am I baking royalty payment directly into my own settlement function so it literally can't be skipped, which matters a lot more if the creator actually cares about enforcement rather than just gesturing at it. For indexing, I wouldn't even consider trying to serve 'browse all active listings sorted by price' from raw chain reads — that needs a subgraph tracking Listing and Sale entities properly. And on the frontend side, I'm careful to design the UX so a user clearly understands which action is free — signing a listing message — versus which action costs them gas and requires a real transaction — buying — because conflating those two in the UI is a classic way to confuse users about what they're actually agreeing to.
commonMistakes: Doesn't address the on-chain-vs-signed-off-chain listing storage tradeoff explicitly
Doesn't address royalty enforcement as an explicit architectural decision
Omits the indexing layer needed for practical listing browsing
Doesn't distinguish signature-based (gas-free) listing creation from on-chain (gas-costing) settlement in the UX
keyPoints: Addresses the on-chain vs. signed-off-chain listing storage tradeoff
Makes an explicit royalty enforcement decision
Includes an indexing layer for practical listing/sale queries
Designs frontend/wallet UX distinguishing gas-free signing from on-chain settlement

questions.title: Designing a DAO Governance System End to End
questions.prompt: Design a complete DAO governance system: the governance token and voting mechanics, the proposal lifecycle, and the treasury/execution layer. What specific design decisions protect against the governance attacks you'd expect at scale?
questions.modelAnswer: The governance token needs checkpointed delegation so voting power at any historical block is queryable, and voting power for any given proposal must be based on a snapshot taken at proposal creation, not live balance, closing the flash-loan governance attack vector entirely. The proposal lifecycle needs a minimum proposal threshold (a minimum token holding to even create a proposal, preventing spam), a defined voting period long enough for genuine deliberation and participation, a quorum requirement so a small, motivated minority can't pass changes when overall participation is low, and ideally a proposal-to-vote delay giving the community time to review before voting opens, closing any single-transaction attack that depends on creating and immediately exploiting a favorable condition. The treasury and execution layer needs a timelock on any passed proposal's execution — even a fully, legitimately passed vote should sit for a delay before executing, giving the community a public window to notice and react to a proposal that turns out to be malicious or badly designed — and the treasury itself should be controlled by a multisig of trusted signers executing only what's been timelock-approved, not a single address, so that neither a single compromised key nor a single successful vote alone is sufficient to move funds. Together, these layers mean an attacker needs to defeat snapshotting, quorum, proposal thresholds, the review delay, the voting period, the timelock, and the multisig all at once — not just one weak link — to actually extract value.
questions.professionalAnswer: I design this as layers, deliberately, because no single mechanism is supposed to carry the whole weight of security on its own. The token itself needs checkpointed delegation so voting power at any historical block is a verifiable lookup, and every proposal's voting power gets locked to a snapshot at creation time, which on its own already kills flash-loan governance attacks outright. On the proposal lifecycle, I want a real proposal threshold so this isn't spammable, a quorum requirement so a quiet week doesn't let a small motivated group push something through nobody else weighed in on, and a delay between proposal creation and voting actually opening, which closes off any attack that depends on creating a favorable condition and immediately exploiting it. Treasury and execution is where I'm most careful — even a vote that passes completely legitimately sits in a timelock before it executes, because that delay is the community's last chance to notice something's wrong before it's irreversible, and the treasury itself is a multisig executing only what's already timelock-approved, never acting on its own judgment. What I like about stacking it this way is that an attacker can't win by breaking just one layer — they'd need to defeat snapshotting, quorum, the review delay, and the timelock all at once, and that's a fundamentally harder problem than finding one weak link in a single-mechanism design.
commonMistakes: Doesn't use snapshot-based voting power, leaving the system open to flash-loan governance attacks
Omits quorum requirements, allowing low-participation votes to pass
Doesn't layer a timelock on top of a passed vote before execution
Puts the treasury under a single address or vote-only control rather than a multisig gated by the timelock
keyPoints: Uses snapshot-based, checkpointed voting power
Includes proposal threshold, quorum, and voting period requirements
Layers a timelock on top of passed votes before execution
Controls the treasury via multisig gated by timelock-approved actions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound proposal lifecycle design (threshold, quorum, delay)

questions.title: Designing Treasury and Timelock Architecture for a DAO
questions.prompt: Specifically for the treasury and timelock layer of a DAO (separate from the voting mechanics), what architectural decisions matter — how funds are custodied, who can queue/execute actions, and how you'd handle an emergency that needs faster-than-normal response?
questions.modelAnswer: Treasury funds should be held by a multisig contract whose signers are a defined, known set of trusted parties (not the governance token holders directly, since 'anyone with enough tokens' isn't the same as 'a vetted signer'), and that multisig should only execute actions that have already passed through governance voting and the timelock, meaning the multisig's role is enforcement of already-approved decisions, not independent decision-making authority. Queueing an action into the timelock should require proof the corresponding proposal actually passed (checked on-chain against the governance contract's recorded outcome, not just trusted from an off-chain claim), and only the timelock contract itself, after its delay elapses, should be able to trigger the multisig's execution — not allowing the multisig signers to bypass the timelock and execute something directly, since that would defeat the entire purpose of the public reaction window. For genuine emergencies (a critical vulnerability requiring an urgent treasury action, like pausing or moving funds to safety), a separate, explicitly-scoped emergency path makes sense — a smaller emergency multisig with a much shorter or zero delay, but deliberately limited to specific defensive actions (pause, not arbitrary fund movement) and requiring a higher signer threshold or public disclosure obligation immediately after use, so the emergency path can't quietly become a backdoor around normal governance for anything beyond genuine emergencies.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I always want crystal clear in a treasury design is: does the multisig have any independent authority, or is it purely an enforcement arm for decisions governance already made? I design toward the latter — the multisig's signers are a known, vetted set, not just 'whoever has enough tokens,' and their job is executing what's already passed a vote and cleared the timelock, nothing more. I make sure queueing into the timelock actually checks on-chain that the corresponding proposal passed, rather than trusting someone's off-chain claim that it did, and critically, I don't let the multisig signers bypass the timelock and execute directly even if they're all in agreement — because the entire point of that delay is giving the public a reaction window, and a bypass path defeats that no matter how well-intentioned the signers are in any given moment. Where it gets genuinely interesting is emergencies — if there's a live critical vulnerability, waiting out a normal governance cycle to pause the protocol is its own kind of negligence. So I'd carve out a separate emergency path with a much shorter delay, but I'd scope it tightly to defensive actions only, pausing, not moving funds anywhere, with a higher signer threshold and a public disclosure requirement the moment it's used, specifically so that narrow emergency door can't quietly turn into a general-purpose way around normal governance.
commonMistakes: Lets the multisig execute independently of the timelock/governance outcome, giving it unchecked authority
Doesn't verify a proposal's actual passage on-chain before allowing it to be queued
Has no distinct emergency path, forcing a slow full-governance cycle even during active incidents
Designs an emergency path broad enough to move arbitrary funds rather than scoped to defensive actions only
keyPoints: Treasury multisig enforces already-approved decisions rather than deciding independently
Verifies proposal passage on-chain before queueing an action
Timelock, not the multisig directly, gates when an approved action can execute
Designs a scoped, accountable emergency path distinct from normal governance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound verification of proposal passage before queueing
Sound, appropriately scoped emergency path design

questions.title: Designing the Indexing Architecture for Marketplace Listings and Sales
questions.prompt: Design the indexing architecture specifically for an NFT marketplace's listings and sales data — what entities you'd model, how you'd keep listing status (active/sold/cancelled) accurate, and how you'd support the query patterns a real marketplace front-end needs.
questions.modelAnswer: The core entities are Listing (mutable, since its status changes from active to sold or cancelled over time) and Sale (immutable, a historical record of a completed transaction), with the Listing entity tracking its current status explicitly rather than relying on consumers to infer status from the absence or presence of related Sale records. Keeping listing status accurate requires mapping handlers for every event that changes a listing's lifecycle — ListingCreated sets status to active, Sale (or Purchased) sets the matching listing's status to sold and creates the Sale record, Cancelled sets status to cancelled — and the handler for each of these needs to correctly look up and update the existing Listing entity by its id rather than only ever creating new entities, which is a common mistake that leaves stale 'active' listings in the index after they've actually sold or been cancelled. Supporting real front-end query patterns (browse active listings for a collection, sorted by price; a user's sale history; a collection's recent sales) requires designing entity fields and relationships with those specific queries in mind from the start — denormalizing collection and seller references onto the Listing and Sale entities directly rather than requiring multiple round-trip queries to resolve relationships, since subgraph GraphQL queries are most efficient when the shape of stored data already matches the shape of the question being asked.
questions.professionalAnswer: I model this as two entities with very different natures — Listing is mutable because its whole job is tracking a status that changes over its life, active to sold or cancelled, and Sale is immutable because it's just a historical fact once it happens. The detail I'd stress most in a design review is that Listing needs an explicit status field — I don't want any consumer having to infer 'is this still active' by checking whether a Sale record happens to exist for it, that's fragile and slow. Every lifecycle event needs its own handler that correctly finds and updates the existing Listing by id — created sets it active, a sale sets it to sold and writes the Sale record, a cancellation sets it cancelled — and the mistake I watch for in code review is a handler that only ever creates new entities and never updates the existing one, because that's exactly how you end up with stale 'active' listings for things that sold weeks ago. The other thing I design around from day one is the actual query patterns the frontend needs — browse active listings for a collection sorted by price, a user's sale history, a collection's recent sales — and I denormalize collection and seller references directly onto Listing and Sale rather than making every query do multiple round trips to resolve a relationship, because GraphQL queries against a subgraph are fastest when the stored shape already matches the question being asked.
commonMistakes: Treats Listing as immutable or doesn't model explicit status, forcing consumers to infer status indirectly
Only creates new entities in handlers rather than updating existing Listing records on status-changing events
Doesn't design entity fields/relationships around the actual front-end query patterns needed
Misses handling one of the lifecycle events (e.g. cancellation) leaving stale data
keyPoints: Correctly models Listing (mutable, status-tracking) vs. Sale (immutable, historical)
Correctly updates existing entities on lifecycle events rather than only creating new ones
Designs fields/relationships around real front-end query patterns
Covers all lifecycle-changing events, not just creation and sale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct handler design for lifecycle events

questions.title: Designing a Multi-Chain Deployment Architecture
questions.prompt: You need to deploy the same protocol to several EVM chains and keep it operating consistently across all of them. Design the architecture for configuration management, cross-chain consistency, and operational monitoring across deployments.
questions.modelAnswer: Configuration management needs a single source of truth — a structured config file or on-chain registry keyed by chain ID — holding every per-chain value (oracle addresses, token addresses, gas assumptions) so deployment scripts read from that source rather than embedding chain-specific values directly in code, which is what makes adding a new chain later a configuration change rather than a code change. Cross-chain consistency for contract addresses is best achieved via CREATE2 with a fixed salt and identical creation code/constructor arguments across chains, so the same logical contract lands at the same address everywhere, simplifying both operational tooling and user-facing documentation that can reference one address instead of a per-chain lookup table. Operational monitoring needs to be chain-aware from the start: a single dashboard aggregating protocol health metrics (TVL, utilization, pending liquidations) across all deployed chains, with alerting thresholds that can be tuned per chain since some chains have meaningfully different liquidity depth, gas economics, or finality characteristics that make a one-size-fits-all alert threshold either too noisy or too insensitive on at least some chains. Governance and upgrade authority also need an explicit per-chain decision: whether each chain has its own independent multisig/timelock (more operationally complex but limits blast radius of a single compromised governance process) or a shared cross-chain governance mechanism (simpler to reason about centrally, but means a single compromised process affects every chain at once).
questions.professionalAnswer: The first architectural call I'd make is treating configuration as data, not code — a single structured file or on-chain registry keyed by chain ID holding every per-chain value, oracle addresses, token addresses, gas assumptions, so adding chain number six later is editing a config entry, not touching deployment code. For address consistency, I'd use CREATE2 with a fixed salt and identical creation code across every chain, specifically so I can tell someone 'the contract is at this one address everywhere' instead of maintaining a per-chain lookup table that's one more thing to keep in sync and one more place for drift to creep in. Monitoring is where I've seen teams get lazy and regret it — a single aggregated dashboard across all chains is necessary, but I push back hard on one-size-fits-all alert thresholds, because a utilization threshold that's perfectly tuned for a deep-liquidity chain is going to be either constantly noisy or completely blind on a thinner one with different gas economics. And governance is a decision I want made explicitly, not by default — do we run independent multisigs per chain, which limits blast radius if one process gets compromised but means more operational overhead, or one shared governance process, which is simpler to reason about but means a single compromise hits every chain simultaneously. I don't think there's a universally right answer there, but I do think not deciding it explicitly, and letting it default to whatever's easiest at deployment time, is a mistake.
commonMistakes: Hardcodes per-chain values instead of driving configuration from a single structured source
Doesn't address cross-chain address consistency (CREATE2) as an explicit architectural decision
Designs monitoring with one-size-fits-all thresholds, ignoring per-chain liquidity/gas differences
Doesn't make an explicit decision about per-chain vs. shared governance authority and its blast-radius tradeoff
keyPoints: Centralizes per-chain configuration in a single structured source
Addresses cross-chain address consistency via CREATE2
Designs chain-aware monitoring with tunable, per-chain thresholds
Makes an explicit, justified decision on per-chain vs. shared governance authority

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound reasoning on governance authority tradeoffs

questions.title: Upgradeable vs. Immutable Contracts: An Architectural Decision Framework
questions.prompt: Design a decision framework for when a protocol should use upgradeable (proxy-based) contracts versus fully immutable ones. What factors actually drive the decision, and how would you apply the framework to a lending protocol versus a simple token vesting contract?
questions.modelAnswer: The decision framework should weigh: how likely genuine logic changes are over the contract's life (a complex, actively-developed protocol with evolving features is more likely to need upgrades than a simple, narrowly-scoped contract that does one well-defined thing forever); how catastrophic an undiscovered bug would be if unfixable (immutability means a critical bug can only be fixed by migration, not an in-place patch, which is a real cost for anything holding significant value); and how much the team is willing to invest in the governance and security required to make upgradeability itself safe (a well-governed upgrade path with multisig and timelock is a real engineering and organizational investment, not a checkbox). Applying this to a lending protocol: lending protocols are complex, tend to add new collateral types and risk parameters over time, and a critical unfixable bug in an immutable version could mean permanent, unrecoverable loss of all deposited funds — this generally favors upgradeability, provided the team invests properly in multisig/timelock-gated upgrades and storage-layout safety tooling. Applying it to a simple token vesting contract: vesting logic is narrow, well-understood, rarely needs to change once deployed, and critically, immutability itself is often a selling point to the people being vested to, since it proves the team can't later change the rules in their own favor — here immutability is usually the better choice, trading upgrade flexibility for a credible, unchangeable commitment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I boil this down to three questions I'd ask about any contract: how likely is it that we'll genuinely need to change the logic later, how bad is it if a bug slips through and we can't fix it in place, and how much are we actually willing to invest in making an upgrade path safe rather than just technically possible. For a lending protocol, my answer leans toward upgradeable pretty quickly — these things grow, new collateral types get added, risk parameters get tuned as the protocol matures, and the cost of an unfixable critical bug is total, unrecoverable loss of everything deposited, which is about as bad as it gets. But I'd only recommend that if the team is genuinely committing to multisig-and-timelock-gated upgrades and real storage-layout tooling, not just slapping a proxy on it and calling it done. For a simple vesting contract, I'd actually argue the other way, and this is the answer that surprises people sometimes — vesting logic is narrow, it's well understood, it basically never needs to change once it's live, and immutability there isn't just a lack of flexibility, it's a feature the recipients actually value, because it's proof the team can't quietly change the unlock terms on them later. I think the mistake is treating this as a technology preference instead of a contract-by-contract judgment call that depends on how complex the logic is and who actually benefits from the guarantee either choice provides.
commonMistakes: Treats the decision as universal (always upgradeable, or always immutable) rather than context-dependent
Doesn't weigh the cost of an unfixable bug against the cost of upgrade-path risk
Doesn't recognize that immutability can be a deliberate credibility/trust feature, not just a limitation
Fails to apply the framework concretely to the two contrasting examples given
keyPoints: Identifies likelihood of needed changes as a key factor
Weighs the cost of an unfixable critical bug against upgrade-path governance investment
Recognizes immutability as a deliberate trust/credibility feature in some contexts
Correctly applies the framework to both the lending protocol and vesting contract examples

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct application to the lending protocol example
Correct application to the vesting contract example

questions.title: Designing the Off-Chain Backend Architecture for a Production dApp
questions.prompt: Design the off-chain backend architecture that a production dApp needs beyond the smart contracts themselves — covering RPC access, event/data indexing, and how the pieces fit together with the frontend. What are the key reliability decisions?
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture needs three distinct layers working together: an RPC access layer with multiple provider failover (never a single RPC provider as a hard dependency, since any provider can and will have outages), an indexing layer (a subgraph or custom indexer) that transforms raw on-chain events into the relational, queryable data the frontend actually needs rather than the frontend ever querying raw chain state directly for anything beyond simple reads, and an event-listening/backend-service layer for anything requiring the application to react to on-chain activity server-side (triggering notifications, running automated logic) rather than just serving reads. Key reliability decisions include: the RPC layer needs health-checking and automatic failover logic, not just a static list of providers; the indexing layer needs monitoring for sync lag (comparing indexed head to chain head) with alerting before users notice stale data, not after; and event-listening services need durable checkpointing and idempotent processing so a crash or restart never silently drops events or double-processes them. The frontend should be designed to degrade gracefully when any one of these layers is briefly unavailable — showing cached or slightly stale data with a clear 'last updated' indicator rather than a hard failure — because in a production system built on top of a probabilistic, occasionally-reorg-prone chain and third-party infrastructure, some degree of transient unavailability in any one layer is a near-certainty, not an edge case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this as three layers that each need their own reliability story, not one blob of 'backend.' The RPC layer never gets to be a single provider as a hard dependency in my designs — every provider has outages, it's not a question of if, so I want health-checking and automatic failover baked in from the start, not a static list someone edits manually after the first incident. The indexing layer is where the frontend should get anything relational or historical from — I don't want the frontend ever querying raw chain state for something a subgraph should be serving — and I want active monitoring on sync lag specifically, comparing the indexed head against the real chain head, with alerting before users notice stale data, not after someone complains. Anything that needs to react to on-chain activity server-side, sending notifications, running automated logic, gets its own event-listening service with durable checkpointing and idempotent processing, because a crash shouldn't silently drop or double-process anything. And then there's the frontend's job in all this — I design it to degrade gracefully, showing slightly stale cached data with an honest 'last updated' timestamp rather than a hard error, because on top of a probabilistic chain and third-party infrastructure, some layer being briefly unavailable isn't an edge case, it's a Tuesday.
commonMistakes: Relies on a single RPC provider with no failover
Has the frontend query raw chain state for data that should come from an indexing layer
Doesn't propose monitoring for indexer sync lag specifically
Doesn't design for graceful degradation when a backend layer is briefly unavailable
keyPoints: Designs RPC access with multi-provider failover
Correctly separates indexing layer responsibilities from raw RPC reads
Proposes concrete reliability measures for each layer (failover, sync-lag monitoring, checkpointing)
Designs for graceful degradation rather than hard failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and layers the three architectural components
Proposes concrete reliability measures per layer
